abstract.p: Cancer continues to be a leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, which necessitates the development of more effective and less toxic therapies. Quinoxaline derivatives, a class of heterocyclic compounds with versatile chemical structures, have emerged as promising candidates for anticancer drug development. These derivatives exhibit a range of biological activities and have shown significant efficacy against various tumors. However, the therapeutic potential of quinoxaline derivatives, particularly in clinical applications, remains underexplored, highlighting the need for further research to optimize their use as anticancer agents. This systematic review aims to provide an updated analysis of quinoxaline derivatives’ anticancer potential, focusing on their mechanisms of action and therapeutic applications in oncology. Following PRISMA guidelines, a thorough search was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed and Science Direct for studies from 2020 to 2024. Relevant keywords were used to identify studies on quinoxaline derivatives and their anticancer properties, resulting in the selection of 77 studies based on pharmacological activity and mechanisms. The review included 77 studies exploring various anticancer activities of quinoxaline derivatives. Key findings indicate that these compounds effectively inhibit cancer cell growth through multiple mechanisms, including the inhibition of topoisomerases, kinases, and other critical proteins involved in cancer progression. Additionally, they demonstrate strong antiproliferative and pro-apoptotic effects across several cancer cell lines, highlighting their broad therapeutic potential. Quinoxaline derivatives represent a promising class of compounds in anticancer therapy due to their diverse biological activities and multiple molecular targets. The development of these derivatives as targeted therapies holds the potential for more effective cancer treatments.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Cancer is globally recognized as a leading cause of mortality, affecting millions of individuals worldwide (World Health Organization, Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, 2024). A worrying increase in cancer mortality is anticipated globally, with an estimated 9.74 million deaths from all forms of cancer expected to occur in 2022 and 10.4 million deaths by 2025 (International Agency for Research on Cancer, 2024). The most diagnosed cancers globally include breast, lung, colorectal, prostate, non-melanoma skin cancers, and stomach cancer, each impacting various body tissues and systems. Cancer is characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells due to genetic and epigenetic changes, leading to the formation of invasive tumors capable of metastasizing through the bloodstream or lymphatic system. The tumor microenvironment, comprising various cells and the extracellular matrix, plays a crucial role in cancer progression. These mutations may be inherited or arise from environmental factors such as tobacco smoke, radiation, and carcinogenic chemicals or through random DNA replication errors (Lewandowska et al., 2019). Current anticancer drugs, such as chemotherapy, remain highly toxic, targeting both healthy and cancerous cells. This lack of specificity results in severe side effects and limits the effectiveness of treatment. While cancer therapies have become more advanced and targeted, ongoing research and development are important to enhance their efficacy, minimize side effects, and provide accessible and personalized treatment plans for all patients.

Quinoxaline, a weakly basic bicyclic compound with the molecular formula C8H6N2, contains fused benzene and pyrazine rings, where nitrogen atoms replace one or more carbon atoms of the naphthalene ring (Husain and Madhesia, 2011). Quinoxaline derivatives are a notable class of heterocyclic compounds that have been extensively studied over the past two decades. Research studies on Quinoxaline found a wide range of biological properties and solidified their potential in medicinal chemistry due to its versatile chemical structure (Khatoon and Abdulmalek, 2021). This led to the development of a broad range of derivatives with multiple biological activities, including antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral, antimalarial, and neurological effects (Husain and Madhesia, 2011). These compounds have demonstrated efficacy against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, with notable potential in inhibiting Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Pereira et al., 2015). Furthermore, quinoxaline derivatives exhibit potent antifungal properties (Tang et al., 2022) and have shown antiviral potential, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, some derivatives showed promising antimalarial activity (Guillon et al., 2017), and others demonstrated central nervous system depressant effects (Olayiwola et al., 2007).

Quinoxaline derivatives are highly recognized as a distinct class of chemotherapeutic agents with significant efficacy against various tumors (Lucaciu et al., 2022). Several cellular targets are specifically inhibited by quinoxaline-based compounds, including topoisomerase, vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR-2), telomerase, farnesyltransferase, tyrosine kinase, and protein kinase CK-11 (Deng et al., 2023). These compounds are particularly effective in targeting breast cancer cell proliferation and metastasis by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and MAPK/ERK pathways, as well as other proteins involved in angiogenesis (Paplomata and O’Regan, 2014). Efficacy has also been demonstrated against ER-positive breast cancer cells by disrupting estrogen-signaling receptors (Moga et al., 2021). Several commercially available drugs containing the quinoxaline moiety have demonstrated significant efficacy in oncology. For example, Echinomycin, a commercially available anticancer agent, inhibits hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), a key factor for tumor growth and survival in low-oxygen conditions commonly found in solid tumors. Echinomycin has been effective against various cancers, including leukemia and lymphoma (Yonekura et al., 2013). Another example is lenvatinib, a multi-kinase inhibitor that targets multiple tyrosine kinases involved in tumor proliferation and metastasis (Padda et al., 2024). These drugs highlight the important role of the quinoxaline scaffold in developing effective cancer therapies.

Since the last systematic review in 2019 (Montana et al., 2019), significant paradigm shifts have emerged. Notably, recent investigations have uncovered novel molecular targets such as bromodomain-containing protein 9 (BRD9), BD1-selective BET proteins, and the glycolytic regulator PFKFB3 targets not addressed in earlier reviews. These discoveries broaden the therapeutic scope of quinoxaline derivatives beyond traditional pathways like Topoisomerase II and classic tyrosine kinase receptors. In parallel, new preclinical and early translational studies have revealed that optimized quinoxaline analogues can inhibit key drivers of angiogenesis such as VEGFR-2 and may help overcome resistance to approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors, including lenvatinib and sorafenib.

This five year update therefore aims to synthesize these latest findings, highlight structure activity relationship advances, and provide an integrated analysis linking emerging molecular targets with evolving clinical strategies, thereby clarifying the novelty and clinical relevance of quinoxaline derivatives in modern anticancer therapy.

sec.title: Background definitions
sec.p: This study was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The search strategy for this systematic review involved selecting studies that specifically investigated the pharmacological activity and underlying mechanisms of quinoxaline derivatives.

sec.title: Data sources and searches
sec.p: A thorough search of English-language scientific literature was performed utilizing two major online databases: MEDLINE/PubMed (National Library of Medicine, n.d.) and ScienceDirect (Elsevier, n.d.). The initial search was conducted without imposing time or language restrictions. Each identified study was meticulously evaluated, with particular attention given to details such as sources, proposed mechanisms of action, dosage/concentration, test systems, and overall conclusions and recommendations.
The literature research involved the following keyword combinations to identify relevant studies:

• “Quinoxaline”, AND “tubulin polymerization inhibitors” OR “topoisomerase” OR “alkylating agents” OR “antifolate agents” OR “antimetabolite agents” OR “tyrosine kinase”, OR “(mTOR, OR Pi3K, OR Akt) “, OR “PARP”; OR “proteasome”.
• “Quinoxaline”, AND “anticancer” OR “Chemotherapy” OR “antiproliferation” OR “antitumor” OR “cytotoxicity
• “Quinoxaline AND cancer treatment”
Searches were conducted within a defined time frame, limiting the final search dates to studies published between 2020 and 2024.

sec.title: Study selection and selection criteria
sec.p: The initial screening of titles and abstracts was conducted independently by two reviewers, who categorized the studies as “yes,” “no,” or “maybe” based on predefined inclusion criteria. Studies marked as “yes” or “maybe” were selected for full-text review. A third reviewer cross-checked the search results for accuracy. The review process was executed in two primary stages, adhering to the eligibility criteria outlined in Table 1.

Duplicate records were identified and removed using Mendeley, and the remaining studies were assessed for eligibility based on their titles and abstracts. In the second stage, the full texts of the selected articles were reviewed, with those not meeting the criteria excluded. Furthermore, the references cited within the included studies were carefully examined to identify any additional relevant research that may have been overlooked during the initial search.

sec.title: Data extraction and risk of bias assessment
sec.p: Two investigators independently assessed and extracted data from the included research studies. When necessary, the authors of the original research were contacted for additional information. Data were abstracted using a pre-designed structured outline, which included the following fields: general information (first author, publication year, country, and study design); study type (in vitro, in vivo, in silico); the chemical name of quinoxaline derivatives; and the mechanism of biological activity (Guyatt et al., 2011). The outcomes of all included studies were evaluated and summarized. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) criteria, adapted for in vitro studies as described by Pavan et al. (2015). Each included study was classified as high, moderate, low, or very low in terms of methodological rigor and reporting quality. Among the 77 studies included in this review, 46.75% were rated as high quality, 36.36% as moderate, and 16.88% as low or very low quality. This distribution highlights that while the majority of the included evidence was of acceptable to strong quality, a substantial proportion of studies still exhibited limitations in experimental design, reproducibility, or reporting clarity.

sec.title: Data extraction process
sec.p: As illustrated in Fig. 1, the database search yielded 459 records. After eliminating duplicates, we identified 343 unique articles. We focused on studies published between 2020 and 2024, which narrowed the selection to 86 articles. In the initial evaluation phase, which involved reviewing titles and abstracts, 2 records were excluded, leaving 84 articles for further analysis. After thoroughly reading the full texts, 7 additional articles were removed. This process culminated in a total of 77 articles included in the review. The articles were critically assessed and categorized based on the pharmacological properties investigated. The categories were arranged in descending order according to the number of articles addressing each mechanism of action (Table 2). Notably, a single manuscript could be included in multiple categories if it evaluated more than one pharmacological activity.

As shown in Fig. 2, the structural representation of quinoxaline derivatives highlights the most frequently studied mechanisms of action identified in the reviewed articles. These include modulation of apoptotic signaling, inhibition of key receptor tyrosine kinases (such as EGFR, VEGFR-2, HER2, and c-Met), disruption of microtubule dynamics via tubulin polymerization inhibition, and DNA intercalation.

sec.title: Growth and proliferation control
sec.p: Quinoxaline derivatives as induction of apoptosis: Apoptosis induction refers to the process of triggering programmed cell death in cancer cells through various molecular mechanisms, often involving the activation of caspases and modulation of pro-apoptotic and anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-2-associated X protein (BAX) and Bcl-2 (Wong, 2011). This process can be initiated via both intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, where the extrinsic lethal stimuli activate caspase-8, leading to downstream activation of caspase-3, while intrinsic stimuli activate BAX/BAK and caspase-9. Table 3 summarizes key findings on the induction of apoptosis by quinoxaline derivatives, including their anticancer activities and IC50 values across different cancer cell lines.

Apoptosis induction by quinoxaline derivatives has been closely associated with scaffold planarity and the ability to engage DNA-dependent death pathways. Within this context (Abbass et al., 2020) reported that compound 22 exhibited pronounced anticancer and apoptosis-inducing activity, particularly against hepatocellular carcinoma cells. The compound demonstrated IC50 values of 10.23 μM, 2.81 μM, and 7.28 μM against colorectal carcinoma (HCT-116), HepG2, and breast cancer (MCF-7) cell lines, respectively. Notably, compound 22 increased apoptotic cell populations in HepG2 cells by more than five-fold compared to untreated controls and markedly upregulated caspase-9 and caspase-3 levels by approximately 7-fold and 10-fold, respectively. Collectively, these findings support the notion that planar quinoxaline scaffolds can efficiently trigger intrinsic apoptotic pathways through DNA intercalation and caspase cascade activation, with enhanced sensitivity observed in hepatocellular carcinoma models.

Hybridization of the quinoxaline scaffold with heterocyclic moieties has been shown to enhance apoptotic potency by modulating key survival pathways. In this regard, quinoxaline–1,3,4-oxadiazole hybrids reported by Ono et al. (2020) demonstrated pronounced antiproliferative and apoptosis-inducing activity in leukemia models. Notably, compound 6c exhibited strong activity against HL-60 cells with an IC50 value of 2.1 ± 0.8 μM, while related analogues such as compound 6d and 3-N-methylpiperazinyl quinoxaline derivatives displayed comparable micromolar potency (IC50 values of 2.3 ± 0.4 μM, 2.9 ± 1.0 μM, and 2.4 ± 0.7 μM, respectively). Mechanistically, RT-PCR analysis revealed a marked reduction in Bcl-2 mRNA expression to less than 10% of untreated controls, indicating that apoptosis induction was mediated through suppression of anti-apoptotic signaling rather than nonspecific cytotoxicity.

Consistent with structure-dependent apoptotic activity observed for substituted quinoxaline derivatives, compounds incorporating optimized electronic features have demonstrated pronounced antiproliferative potency across multiple cancer cell lines. In this context, quinoxaline derivative 15f reported by Fayed et al. (2020) exhibited strong activity against HCT-116, HepG-2, and MCF-7 cells, with IC50 values of 1.62 μM, 1.46 μM, and 2.04 μM, respectively. This compound markedly enhanced apoptotic signaling, as evidenced by significant upregulation of activated caspase-3 (11.53-fold) and pro-apoptotic BAX protein levels (10-fold), alongside downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 (3.8-fold). Similarly, compound 14b displayed potent cytotoxicity against the same cancer cell lines (IC50 values of 1.96 μM, 1.12 μM, and 2.38 μM, respectively) and induced apoptosis through modulation of caspase-3, BAX, and Bcl-2 expression. Collectively, these findings underscore the role of rational substitution on the quinoxaline scaffold in enhancing intrinsic apoptotic pathway activation rather than nonspecific cytotoxicity.

Moderately substituted quinoxaline derivatives have been shown to maintain consistent antiproliferative activity across diverse epithelial cancer models. In this context, compounds 16, 17, and 20 reported by Abu-Hashem et al. (2021) exhibited comparable cytotoxic profiles against nasopharyngeal (CNE2), oral (KB), breast (MCF-7), and gastric (MGC-803) carcinoma cell lines. Compound 16 demonstrated IC50 values of 11.9, 10.9, 11.6, and 11.5 μM against CNE2, KB, MCF-7, and MGC-803 cells, respectively, while compound 17 showed similar potency (IC50 values of 11.8, 10.8, 11.5, and 11.3 μM). Notably, compound 20 displayed the highest overall efficacy among this series, with IC50 values of 11.6, 10.5, 11.3, and 10.9 μM across the same cell lines. Mechanistic investigations revealed that these derivatives induced apoptosis through modulation of key intrinsic pathway regulators, including caspase-3 activation, BAX upregulation, and Bcl-2 suppression, underscoring the contribution of scaffold optimization to balanced cytotoxic and apoptotic activity.

Further studies by Alanazi et al. (2021a) demonstrated that compound 11e showed significant antiproliferative activities against HepG2 and MCF-7 cancer cell lines, with IC50 values of 2.1 μM and 2.7 μM, respectively. This compound caused 49.14% apoptosis in HepG2 cells, compared to 9.71% in normal cells. Mechanistically, 11e dramatically enhanced pro-apoptotic proteins caspase-3 (2.34-fold), caspase-9 (2.34-fold), and BAX (3.14-fold), while lowering anti-apoptotic Bcl-2. Furthermore, 11e inhibited HepG2 cell development in the G2/M phase, raising the proportion of cells in this phase from 18.24% to 46.62%. Compounds 11g, 12e, 12g, and 12k have shown promising cytotoxic activity against tested cell lines, with IC50 values ranging from 3.8 to 9.8 μM. These quinoxaline derivatives induced apoptosis through modulation of key proteins in the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway, demonstrating their potential as anticancer agents targeting apoptosis induction.

Selective apoptosis induction by quinoxaline derivatives has been linked to their ability to preferentially target cancer cells while sparing normal tissue. In this context, compound 11e reported by Alanazi et al. (2021a) exhibited significant antiproliferative activity against HepG2 and MCF-7 cancer cell lines, with IC50 values of 2.1 μM and 2.7 μM, respectively. Notably, 11e induced apoptosis in 49.14% of HepG2 cells compared to only 9.71% in normal cells, indicating a favorable selectivity profile. Mechanistic studies revealed substantial upregulation of intrinsic apoptotic markers, including caspase-3 and caspase-9 (2.34-fold each) and BAX (3.14-fold), accompanied by downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. In addition to apoptosis induction, 11e caused pronounced G2/M cell cycle arrest, increasing the proportion of HepG2 cells in this phase from 18.24% to 46.62%. Supporting this structure–activity trend, related derivatives (11g, 12e, 12g, and 12k) also demonstrated promising cytotoxic activity, with IC50 values ranging from 3.8 to 9.8 μM, collectively highlighting the capacity of optimized quinoxaline scaffolds to trigger mitochondrial pathway–mediated apoptosis in cancer cells.

Structure-driven optimization of quinoxaline derivatives has been shown to markedly enhance apoptotic potency in hepatocellular carcinoma models. In this context, quinoxaline derivatives reported by Ma et al. (2021), particularly compound 6c, demonstrated high antiproliferative activity against HepG-2 and HuH-7 cell lines, with IC50 values of 1.53 μM and 3.06 μM, respectively. This compound significantly increased apoptotic cell populations, elevating early- and late-stage apoptosis by 9.98-fold and 10.81-fold, respectively, compared to control groups. Related analogues, including compounds 6g and 12, also exhibited strong cytotoxic effects, with IC50 values ranging from 1.99 to 3.08 μM across the same cell lines. Mechanistic investigations indicated that these compounds induce apoptosis through upregulation of the pro-apoptotic Bax protein and suppression of the anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 protein, alongside cell cycle arrest in the G0/G1 and S phases. Notably, the presence of electron-withdrawing substituents, such as chloro groups, in combination with the quinoxaline core structure appears to be a key determinant of enhanced apoptotic activity in this series.

Nanostructured delivery of quinoxaline-based systems has emerged as an effective strategy to enhance apoptotic selectivity toward cancer cells while minimizing toxicity to normal tissue. In this context, thiophene–quinoxaline–based conjugated polymer nanoparticles (CPNs), particularly T2fQf and T2fQ2f, reported by Koralli et al. (2021), demonstrated pronounced apoptosis-inducing activity in breast cancer models. Among these systems, nanoprecipitated T2fQf CPNs exhibited the most promising performance, achieving efficient cellular uptake in triple-negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231) with approximately 80% internalization and inducing a more than 10-fold increase in late apoptotic cell populations compared to untreated controls. Importantly, these nanoparticles displayed selective cytotoxicity, as higher concentrations (0.53–1.59 μg/mL) markedly increased apoptosis in cancer cells while exerting only modest effects on normal breast epithelial cells (MCF-10A). Mechanistically, the observed selectivity is likely attributable to preferential intracellular uptake and activation of apoptotic pathways within malignant cells, underscoring the potential of quinoxaline-based nanostructures to improve therapeutic selectivity.

Optimization of quinoxaline derivatives through targeted substitution has been shown to modulate apoptotic signaling and enhance antiproliferative efficacy. In this context, compound 25d reported by Alsaif et al. (2021a) demonstrated notable cytotoxic activity against MCF-7 and HepG2 cells, with IC50 values of 7.2 ± 0.6 μM and 4.1 ± 0.4 μM, respectively. This compound effectively promoted apoptosis by increasing the BAX/Bcl-2 ratio by 3.81-fold and elevating caspase-3 and caspase-9 levels by 1.96- and 1.82-fold, respectively, compared to the control group. Structurally related analogues, including compounds 25e and 25i, also exhibited appreciable antiproliferative activity, with IC50 values ranging from 7.8 to 10.3 μM across the same cancer cell lines. Collectively, these findings indicate that fine-tuning substituent patterns on the quinoxaline scaffold can enhance intrinsic apoptotic pathway activation through coordinated regulation of pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins and caspase signaling.

Fused triazolo–quinoxaline scaffolds have emerged as particularly effective frameworks for apoptosis induction due to their enhanced structural rigidity and target engagement. In this context, derivatives of [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline reported by Alsaif et al. (2021b) demonstrated pronounced antiproliferative and apoptosis-inducing activity in breast and liver cancer models. Notably, compound 19a exhibited strong cytotoxic effects against MCF-7 and HepG2 cells, with IC50 values of 8.2 μM and 5.4 μM, respectively, and significantly promoted apoptosis by increasing the Bax/Bcl-2 ratio by 4.87-fold while elevating caspase-3 and caspase-9 levels by 2.44- and 2.69-fold compared to control cells. Structurally related analogues, including compounds 22b and 22g, also displayed comparable antiproliferative potency, with IC50 values ranging from 6.5 to 10.3 μM across the same cell lines. Mechanistic insights indicate that apoptosis induction by these derivatives is mediated through coordinated modulation of pro- and anti-apoptotic proteins and activation of caspase cascades, underscoring the critical role of the triazolo–quinoxaline core and phenyl substituent patterns in governing apoptotic efficacy.

Highly fused bis-triazolo–quinoxaline architectures have demonstrated enhanced capacity to activate intrinsic apoptotic pathways through cooperative modulation of key regulatory proteins. In this context, bis([1,2,4]triazolo)[4,3-a:3′,4′-c]quinoxaline derivatives reported by Alanazi et al. (2022) exhibited encouraging apoptosis-inducing activity in breast and liver cancer models. Among this series, compound 23j showed pronounced antiproliferative potency against MCF-7 and HepG2 cells, with IC50 values of 10.3 μM and 6.4 μM, respectively, and induced a marked increase in apoptotic cell populations in HepG2 cells (33.05%) compared with control cells (7.07%). Mechanistic analysis revealed substantial upregulation of pro-apoptotic markers, including caspase-3 (1.36-fold), caspase-9 (2.80-fold), and BAX (1.65-fold), alongside significant downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2 (2.63-fold), resulting in an elevated BAX/Bcl-2 ratio of 4.34. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of the bis-triazolo–quinoxaline scaffold and phenyl ring substitution patterns in driving caspase-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells.

Highly planar acenaphthoquinoxaline scaffolds have been shown to exert potent anticancer activity through multimodal mechanisms involving DNA interaction and oxidative stress. In this context, 9-arylacenaphtho[1,2-b]quinoxaline derivatives reported by Babu and Paira (2021) demonstrated notable antiproliferative efficacy across multiple cancer cell lines. Among this series, compound 5a exhibited the strongest activity, with IC50 values of 1.97 μM, 3.06 μM, and 22.01 μM against cervical (HeLa), breast (MCF-7), and glioblastoma (U87MG) cells, respectively. Mechanistic investigations revealed that compound 5a induces cancer cell death through a combination of DNA intercalation, reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and inhibition of cell migration, with apoptosis confirmed by morphological changes and DNA fragmentation assays. Structurally, the rigid and planar acenaphthoquinoxaline core facilitates efficient insertion between DNA base pairs, while variation in aryl substituents modulates lipophilicity and cellular uptake, underscoring the importance of scaffold planarity and peripheral substitution in governing anticancer potency.

Hybridization of the quinoxaline core with benzimidazole moieties has been shown to enhance cytotoxic efficacy through activation of multiple apoptotic pathways. In this context, the quinoxaline–benzimidazole hybrid compound 5l reported by Ommi et al. (2023) exhibited pronounced cytotoxicity against lung cancer (A549) cells, with an IC50 value of 4.37 ± 0.09 μM. Mechanistic evaluation demonstrated that compound 5l induces apoptosis through multiple pathways, as evidenced by acridine orange/ethidium bromide (AO/EB) and 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) staining, which revealed characteristic apoptotic features including cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, and nuclear fragmentation. These findings further support the role of scaffold hybridization in promoting apoptosis-mediated anticancer activity.

Indolo–quinoxaline frameworks incorporating Mannich base functionalities have been shown to exert cytotoxic effects through combined kinase inhibition and apoptosis induction. In this context, the indolo[2,3-b]quinoxaline–Mannich adduct compound 6q reported by Chowdhary et al. (2023) demonstrated measurable cytotoxic activity against colorectal cancer (HT-29) cells, with an IC50 value of 31.36 μM. Apoptosis induction was confirmed through Annexin V/7-amino-actinomycin D (Annexin V/7-AAD) analysis, which revealed that 42.1% of treated cells underwent apoptotic death, and further supported by caspase 3/7 activation, with 28.95% of cells displaying caspase-mediated apoptosis. Mechanistically, molecular docking studies indicated that compound 6q binds to the c-Met kinase at the colchicine-binding site, forming hydrogen-bond interactions with Met1160 and Tyr1159. Notably, the presence of cyclic amine groups, such as piperidine and pyrrolidine, on both the indole core and side chain was found to positively influence activity and selectivity. Collectively, these findings suggest that compound 6q induces apoptosis in colorectal cancer cells through disruption of c-Met kinase signaling in conjunction with caspase-dependent apoptotic pathways.

Potent quinoxaline derivatives capable of simultaneously targeting DNA-processing enzymes and apoptotic signaling pathways have demonstrated promising anticancer efficacy in both in vitro and in vivo models. In this context, compound IV reported by Elsakka et al. (2025) exhibited strong cytotoxic activity against human prostate cancer (PC-3) cells, with an IC50 value of 2.11 μM. Apoptosis induction was confirmed by Annexin V/Propidium iodide (Annexin V/PI) staining, which revealed that 43.56% of treated cells underwent apoptotic death, alongside pronounced G2/M cell cycle arrest. Mechanistic investigations showed that compound IV effectively inhibited topoisomerase II activity (IC50=7.529 μM), a finding further supported by molecular docking studies demonstrating binding to the enzyme’s active site. At the molecular level, western blot analysis revealed dose-dependent upregulation of pro-apoptotic proteins, including p53, caspase-3, and caspase-8, accompanied by downregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein Bcl-2. Importantly, in vivo evaluation in a mouse model bearing Ehrlich solid tumors demonstrated a significant reduction in tumor size and weight following treatment. Collectively, these results indicate that compound IV induces apoptosis in prostate cancer cells through coordinated inhibition of topoisomerase II and modulation of intrinsic and extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathways.

Strategic modification of quinoxaline aryl ether derivatives has been shown to enhance anticancer efficacy through simultaneous kinase inhibition and activation of apoptotic pathways. In this context, compound FQ, a quinoxaline aryl ether derivative reported by Nakka et al. (2024), exhibited pronounced cytotoxic activity against triple-negative breast cancer (MDA-MB-231) cells, with an IC50 value of 8.01 μM. Apoptosis induction was confirmed by Annexin V/7-AAD analysis, which demonstrated that 21.4% of cells underwent apoptosis following exposure to 10 μM FQ for 48 hours, while caspase-3/7 assays revealed a higher apoptotic population (41.8%), indicating caspase-dependent cell death. Mechanistically, compound FQ was shown to inhibit c-Met kinase signaling, as evidenced by reduced Akt phosphorylation. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations further supported stable binding of FQ within the c-Met kinase active site through hydrogen-bond interactions with Arg1086 and aromatic hydrogen bonding with Met1160 and Pro1158. Notably, SAR analysis identified the presence of a 4-fluorophenoxy substituent and a free piperazine moiety as critical contributors to biological activity. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that compound FQ induces apoptosis in breast cancer cells through coordinated inhibition of c-Met kinase signaling and activation of caspase-mediated apoptotic pathways.

Structure-guided optimization of indolo–quinoxaline derivatives has been shown to enhance antiproliferative and apoptosis-inducing activity across multiple cancer models. In this context, compound 27 reported by Malah et al. (2024) emerged as the most potent candidate among a series of evaluated derivatives (22–29), demonstrating superior inhibition of cancer cell proliferation. This compound exhibited strong antiproliferative activity against HCT-116, HepG-2, and MCF-7 cell lines and induced the highest level of apoptosis in HepG-2 liver cancer cells. Cell cycle analysis revealed that the presence of the 6-((1H-1,2,3-triazol-4-yl)methyl)-6H-indolo[2,3-b]quinoxaline moiety resulted in pronounced cell cycle arrest primarily in the S phase, with additional accumulation in the G0/G1 phase. Furthermore, Annexin V/fluorescein isothiocyanate (Annexin V-FITC) staining confirmed substantial apoptotic activity in treated HepG-2 cells. Collectively, these findings indicate that compound 27 effectively activates apoptotic signaling pathways, particularly in liver cancer cells, highlighting the critical role of indolo–quinoxaline–triazole hybridization in driving enhanced anticancer efficacy.

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline derivatives are potent inducers of apoptosis across multiple cancer cell lines, mainly through the modulation of caspase cascades and the BAX/Bcl-2 axis. A recurring structure–activity relationship (SAR) can be observed, where electron-withdrawing substituents such as chloro and fluoro on the phenyl ring and triazolo-quinoxaline scaffolds enhance apoptotic activity, while the presence of piperazine or methylamino groups tends to improve cell permeability and potency. In terms of specificity, hepatocellular carcinoma (HepG2) and breast cancer (MCF-7) cells appear particularly sensitive, although promising effects have also been reported in prostate, colorectal, and leukemia models, suggesting broad multi-target potential. Despite these advances, most studies remain limited to in vitro assays, and the precise apoptotic pathways (intrinsic vs. extrinsic) are not consistently distinguished, with few directly comparing caspase-8 versus caspase-9 activation. Future research should prioritize mechanistic dissection of these pathways, in vivo validation, and structure optimization to improve selectivity and therapeutic index.

sec.title: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors
sec.p: Quinoxaline derivatives as EGFR/ HER2 inhibitors : Inhibiting the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is considered one of the most promising approaches for cancer treatment (Zubair and Bandyopadhyay, 2023). Multiple strategies targeting EGFR have progressed to clinical trials, demonstrating the potential of this approach. Research shows that blocking EGFR is a critical factor in modulating cell signaling pathways that control cell growth, apoptosis, angiogenesis, and metastasis (Sharma et al., 2021). Table 4 summarizes key findings from these studies, highlighting the most effective compounds.

Non-covalent imidazo[1,2-a]quinoxaline scaffolds have demonstrated strong potential as epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors through effective suppression of ATP-dependent EGFR phosphorylation. In this context, a series of imidazoquinoxaline derivatives reported by Kumar et al. (2021) exhibited potent EGFR-WT inhibitory activity, with compounds 6b, 7h, 7j, 9a, and 9c achieving IC50 values of 211.22, 222.21, 193.18, 223.32, and 221.53 nM, respectively—comparable to the reference drug erlotinib (IC50=221.03 nM). Importantly, the translational relevance of these findings was supported by subsequent in vivo evaluation of compound 6b in a non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) xenograft model. As reported by Bhat et al. (2022), administration of compound 6b, particularly at a high dose (30 mg/kg), resulted in significant suppression of tumor volume and reduction in average tumor weight in A549 tumor–bearing nude mice. Histopathological analysis revealed pronounced cytotoxic damage in tumors treated with high-dose 6b, comparable to gefitinib, while tumor growth inhibition (TGI) and Kaplan–Meier survival analyses confirmed improved survival outcomes in these groups. Mechanistically, immunoblotting studies demonstrated upregulation of phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) expression alongside downregulation of Akt signaling in 6b-treated tissues, a finding of particular significance given the established role of PTEN loss and Akt overactivation in EGFR inhibitor resistance. Collectively, these results indicate that compound 6b not only exhibits potent EGFR inhibition in vitro but also achieves meaningful antitumor efficacy in vivo through modulation of EGFR-driven signaling pathways, highlighting its promise as a lead candidate for further development in NSCLC.

Rational optimization of quinoxaline derivatives has yielded compounds with strong inhibitory activity against both wild-type and mutant EGFR kinases. In this context, a focused series of quinoxaline analogues reported by Fayed et al. (2021) demonstrated potent inhibition of EGFR-WT and EGFR L858R tyrosine kinase in MCF-7 cells. Notably, all evaluated compounds exhibited sub-2 μM inhibitory activity against EGFR-WT, underscoring the suitability of the quinoxaline scaffold for EGFR targeting. Among this series, compound 6 displayed the highest potency, with an IC50 value of 63.70 nM, comparable to the reference drug erlotinib. Compounds 7b, 7d, and 3a also showed strong inhibitory activity, with IC50 values of 0.075, 0.957, 1.34, and 1.547 μM, respectively. Collectively, these findings highlight the capacity of appropriately substituted quinoxaline derivatives to achieve nanomolar-to-low micromolar EGFR inhibition, including activity against clinically relevant EGFR mutations.

Systematic functionalization of the quinoxaline core has enabled the identification of derivatives with pronounced EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitory activity. In this context, a series of newly synthesized quinoxaline derivatives reported by Ahmed et al. (2022) were screened for their in vitro anticancer potential, with selected compounds further evaluated against EGFR-TK using erlotinib as a reference inhibitor. Among the tested analogues, compounds 4a and 13 emerged as the most potent EGFR inhibitors, exhibiting IC50 values of 0.3 and 0.4 μM, respectively. Compound 11 demonstrated moderate activity with an IC50 value of 0.6 μM, while compound 5 showed comparatively lower potency (IC50=0.9 μM). Collectively, these results indicate that appropriate functional modification of the quinoxaline scaffold can yield low micromolar to sub-micromolar EGFR inhibition, reinforcing the potential of this chemical class as a source of effective EGFR-targeted anticancer agents.

Structure-based molecular docking analyses have provided further insight into the EGFR inhibitory potential of quinoxaline derivatives. In this context, a series of quinoxaline analogues (IVa–n) reported by Badithapuram et al. (2022) were evaluated for their binding affinity toward the EGFR receptor. Among these compounds, IVd, bearing a bromine substituent, emerged as the most potent binder, exhibiting a predicted inhibition constant of 1.53 nM against EGFR (PDB ID: 4HJO). Docking studies revealed that IVdestablishes two key hydrogen-bond interactions with residues LYS721 and MET769, with bond lengths of 1.88 and 2.50 Å, respectively. These findings highlight the critical role of halogen substitution in enhancing EGFR binding affinity and stabilizing ligand–receptor interactions, further supporting quinoxaline derivatives as promising EGFR-targeted anticancer candidates.

Evaluation of quinoxaline-linked 1,3,4-oxadiazole derivatives has further expanded the scope of EGFR-targeted inhibition within this chemical class. In this context, a set of selected derivatives reported by Osmaniye et al. (2022) were assessed for EGFR kinase inhibitory activity using a commercial fluorometric assay (Human EGFR ELISA Kit), with erlotinib employed as a reference inhibitor. Among the tested compounds, 3e emerged as the most potent EGFR inhibitor, exhibiting an IC50 value of 0.958 ± 0.105 μM. In comparison, compounds 3j, 3g, and 3h demonstrated lower inhibitory potency, with IC50 values of 3.357 ± 0.234 μM, 20.254 ± 0.985 μM, and 31.158 ± 1.235 μM, respectively. Collectively, these results highlight 3eas a promising lead compound within the oxadiazole–quinoxaline series for EGFR kinase inhibition, while underscoring the influence of structural variation on inhibitory efficacy.

Hybridization of quinoxaline scaffolds with sulfur-containing heterocycles and sulfonamide moieties has been shown to markedly enhance EGFR inhibitory potency. In this context, a series of 1,3-dithiolo[4,5-b]quinoxaline–sulfonamide hybrids reported by Ismail et al. (2023) demonstrated strong activity against both wild-type and mutant EGFR. Notably, compound 12 exhibited superior inhibitory potency toward EGFR-WT and the clinically relevant EGFR L858R mutant, with IC50 values of 0.19 ± 0.009 μM and 0.026 ± 0.001 μM, respectively. These results underscore the effectiveness of dithiolo–quinoxaline–sulfonamide hybridization in achieving sub-micromolar to nanomolar EGFR inhibition, highlighting compound 12 as a highly promising lead for targeting EGFR-driven cancers.

Design and functional diversification of quinoxalinone-based pyrazole hybrids have yielded derivatives with promising anticancer and EGFR inhibitory activity. In this context, a series of quinoxalinone–pyrazole derivatives (4a–h) reported by Theodore et al. (2023) demonstrated notable antiproliferative effects, with compounds 4e and 4h exhibiting anticancer activity comparable to the reference drug sorafenib. Further kinase-focused evaluation revealed that compounds 4f and 4g effectively inhibited EGFR kinase activity in vitro, with IC50 values ranging from 1.93 to 4.28 μM. Collectively, these findings suggest that incorporation of a pyrazole moiety into the quinoxalinone framework can confer dual anticancer and EGFR inhibitory properties, while highlighting the influence of specific substitution patterns on kinase-targeted activity.

Allyl substitution on the quinoxaline scaffold has been shown to enhance EGFR inhibitory activity through favorable modulation of kinase–ligand interactions. In this context, the N-allyl quinoxaline derivative reported by Nafie et al. (2024), compound 8, exhibited promising EGFR inhibition, with an IC50 value of 0.088 μM, closely comparable to the reference inhibitor sorafenib (IC50=0.056 μM). These results highlight the potential of N-allyl modification as an effective strategy for achieving sub-micromolar EGFR inhibition within the quinoxaline class.

Hybridization of the quinoxaline core with sulfonyl-1,2,4-triazole moieties has emerged as an effective strategy for enhancing EGFR inhibitory activity. In this context, a series of quinoxaline–sulfonyl–1,2,4-triazole hybrids (5a–n) reported by Dasari et al. (2022) were designed and synthesized through a systematic stepwise approach. In silico evaluation of selected derivatives (5b, 5d, 5g, 5j, and 5k) against the EGFR receptor revealed that compound 5j exhibited the strongest binding affinity toward EGFR (PDB ID: 4HJO). Importantly, subsequent biological evaluation demonstrated that compounds 5j and 5g displayed superior tyrosine kinase EGFR inhibitory activity compared to the reference drug erlotinib. Collectively, these findings highlight quinoxaline–sulfonyl–triazole hybridization as a promising design strategy for the development of potent EGFR-targeted anticancer agents.

Conjugation of the quinoxaline scaffold with piperazine and oxazole amide functionalities has been shown to enhance both antiproliferative activity and EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibition. In this context, a series of quinoxaline–piperazine–oxazole amide conjugates (6a–n) reported by Ferazoddin et al. (2024) were evaluated for their anticancer activity against multiple human cancer cell lines, including PC-3, MCF-7, DU-145, and A549, using erlotinib as a reference drug. Notably, compounds 6c, 6h, 6i, and 6n exhibited superior cytotoxic potency compared with erlotinib across all tested cell lines. Subsequent EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibition assays further confirmed the enhanced activity of this subset, with compounds 6n, 6h, and 6idemonstrating stronger EGFR inhibitory effects than erlotinib, achieving IC50 values of 0.28, 0.31, and 0.36 μM, respectively. Collectively, these findings underscore the value of piperazine–oxazole amide conjugation in optimizing quinoxaline-based scaffolds for potent EGFR-targeted anticancer activity.

Conjugation of quinoxaline scaffolds with 1,2,4-triazole-3-amide motifs has further expanded their potential as EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. In this context, quinoxaline–1,2,4-triazole–3-amide conjugates reported by Ravula et al. (2024) demonstrated notable EGFR inhibitory activity in vitro. Among the evaluated derivatives, 3,5-dimethoxy-N-(5-{[2-oxoquinoxalin-1(2H)-yl]methyl}-4H-1,2,4-triazol-3-yl)benzamide and 4-methoxy-N-(5-{[2-oxoquinoxalin-1(2H)-yl]methyl}-4H-1,2,4-triazol-3-yl)benzamide emerged as the most potent compounds, exhibiting higher tyrosine kinase EGFR inhibition compared to the reference drug etoposide. These findings further support the role of triazole–amide hybridization in enhancing EGFR-targeted activity within quinoxaline-based anticancer agents.

Incorporation of triazole moieties into indolo–quinoxaline frameworks has been shown to enhance cytotoxic potency and EGFR-targeted interactions. In this context, a series of hexahydro-6H-indolo[2,3-b]quinoxaline derivatives incorporating a triazole unit, reported by El Malah et al. (2024a), demonstrated superior cytotoxic activity against selected human cancer cell lines. Notably, compound 15 exhibited strong binding affinity toward the EGFR kinase domain, as revealed by molecular interaction analysis. The binding was primarily driven by favorable van der Waals energy contributions, resulting in substantial binding free energies in the gas phase, reaching values as low as −83.06 kcal/mol. These findings highlight the role of triazole-functionalized indolo–quinoxaline scaffolds in stabilizing EGFR interactions and further support their potential as effective EGFR-targeted anticancer agents.

The human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) plays a major role in the signal transduction pathways of cell division Fig. 3, and several investigations have reported the overexpression of HER2 in breast cancer patients (Swain et al., 2023).

Given the pivotal role of HER2 in driving breast cancer progression, its inhibition has emerged as an attractive therapeutic strategy. In this context, structurally diverse 2-aryl quinoxaline derivatives synthesized by Wadhwani et al. (2024) were evaluated for their potential to target the HER2 receptor using in silico approaches. Molecular docking studies revealed that compounds 3b, 3f, 3g, 3h, and 3k exhibited notable binding affinity toward the HER2 protein (PDB ID: 3PPO). Among these candidates, compound 3k demonstrated the strongest interaction, achieving the highest binding energy (−7.70 kcal/mol), suggesting a favorable and stable ligand–receptor complex. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of 2-aryl quinoxaline scaffolds, particularly compound 3k, as promising leads for the development of HER2-targeted anticancer agents.

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline-based EGFR/HER2 inhibitors exhibit strong enzyme and cellular inhibition, with several derivatives achieving sub-micromolar to nanomolar potency. For example, imidazo[1,2-a]quinoxaline analogues inhibited EGFR-WT in the ~200 nM range comparable to erlotinib, and compound 6b showed in vivo efficacy in an NSCLC xenograft model. Other studies reported even lower IC50 values (e.g., 63.7 nM; 0.19/0.026 µM for EGFR-WT/L858R; 0.088 µM), supporting the scaffold’s potential. SAR trends consistently highlight the contribution of sulfonamide, oxadiazole, and triazole moieties in enhancing kinase affinity and potency. Recent reviews confirm that quinoxaline derivatives are emerging as a versatile platform for kinase inhibition, with some studies incorporating kinase selectivity panels to evaluate off-target liabilities. Nevertheless, important gaps remain: most investigations rely on in vitro data, only a few include in vivo validation, and systematic evaluation of resistance mechanisms or HER2-specific selectivity in clinically relevant models is still limited. Future research should therefore expand comparative studies with approved TKIs, assess long-term resistance, and conduct broader kinase profiling to clarify translational potential.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as VEGFR inhibitors
sec.p: VEGFR inhibitors are drugs specifically targeting the VEGFR family, which is integral to angiogenesis (Shibuya, 2011). By blocking VEGFR, these inhibitors can effectively cut off the blood supply to tumors, thereby preventing their growth and spread (Shibuya, 2011). The VEGFR family has three primary types: VEGFR-1 (Flt-1), VEGFR-2 (KDR/Flk-1), and VEGFR-3 (Flt-4) (Shibuya, 2011). Numerous studies have highlighted the potential of quinoxaline derivatives as VEGFR inhibitors, showcasing their promise in cancer treatment, as summarized in Table 5, which details the anti-cancer effects of these compounds across various cancer cell lines.

Targeting angiogenic signaling through VEGFR-2 inhibition has emerged as a key strategy in the development of quinoxaline-based anticancer agents. In this context, quinoxaline-3-propamide derivatives reported by El-Adl et al. (2021b) demonstrated potent VEGFR-2 inhibitory activity. Selected cytotoxic candidates, compounds 8, 9, and 14, were evaluated against VEGFR-2 using sorafenib as a reference inhibitor and exhibited strong inhibitory effects with IC50 values ranging from 0.076 to 0.131 μM. Among these, compound 14 emerged as the most potent VEGFR-2 inhibitor, achieving an IC50 value of 0.076 μM, comparable to sorafenib and approximately 1.83-fold more potent than sunitinib. Beyond enzymatic inhibition, compound 14 significantly reduced VEGFR-2 expression and lowered VEGF-A levels in MCF-7 cells compared to untreated controls, supporting its antiangiogenic potential. Collectively, these findings highlight quinoxaline-3-propamide scaffolds, particularly compound 14, as promising leads for angiogenesis inhibition and potential in vivo tumor suppression.

Quinoxaline derivatives have also demonstrated exceptional potency as VEGFR-2 inhibitors, reinforcing their relevance in antiangiogenic drug design. In this context, a series of quinoxaline-based compounds reported by Alanazi et al. (2021a) exhibited remarkable VEGFR-2 inhibitory activity. Notably, compound 21aemerged as the most potent inhibitor, achieving an IC50 value of 3.8 nM, which is closely comparable to the reference drug sorafenib (IC50=3.12 nM). In addition, related derivatives, including compounds 19b, 20a, 21b, and 21c, also displayed strong VEGFR-2 inhibition, with IC50 values ranging from 4.3 to 6.1 nM. Importantly, a strong correlation was observed between VEGFR-2 inhibition and antiproliferative activity against MCF-7 and HepG2 cell lines, with compound 21a showing pronounced inhibitory effects at both the enzymatic and cellular levels. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of optimized quinoxaline scaffolds to achieve nanomolar VEGFR-2 inhibition coupled with effective anticancer activity.

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline derivatives act as potent VEGFR-2 inhibitors, with several compounds exhibiting nanomolar activity, in some cases surpassing reference drugs like sorafenib. SAR analysis reveals that substitutions with halogens and heteroaryl groups on the quinoxaline core significantly improve VEGFR binding affinity and antiproliferative potency. These inhibitors show strong activity against breast, liver, and colorectal cancer cells, with notable selectivity against cancer over normal cells. Importantly, some compounds exhibit dual VEGFR inhibition and cytotoxicity, supporting multi-target potential. However, most findings are limited to cell-based assays, and pharmacokinetic profiles are rarely reported. Future directions should emphasize in vivo angiogenesis models, resistance profiling, and evaluation of drug-like properties to advance these leads toward clinical development.

sec.title: DNA inhibitors
sec.p: DNA intercalators targeting Topoisomerase II (Topo II) are crucial in cancer therapy due to their ability to convert Topo II into a DNA-damaging agent (Burden and Osheroff, 1998). These drugs, which bind non-covalently to DNA, induce structural distortions that disrupt replication and transcription processes, ultimately leading to cell death (Berger et al., 1996) Intercalators typically feature planar aromatic systems that insert between DNA base pairs (Hevener et al., 2018). Topoisomerases, including Topo I and Topo II, manage DNA supercoiling by creating transient breaks in the DNA strands. Topo I cuts one strand, while Topo II cuts both strands. Inhibitors of these enzymes, particularly Topo II poisons, are effective because they stabilize the transient DNA breaks, causing extensive damage (Hevener et al., 2018). Quinoxaline derivatives are prominent in this context as they serve as the backbone for many DNA intercalators and Topo II inhibitors. Research has focused on developing new quinoxaline-based compounds with enhanced anticancer activities by integrating various functional groups to improve DNA binding and intercalation efficiency. These compounds are evaluated through in vitro assays and molecular docking studies to determine their antiproliferative effects and binding affinities, aiming to optimize their therapeutic potential against cancer, as summarized in Table 6.

Optimization of quinoxaline-based DNA intercalators has highlighted the importance of scaffold planarity and aromatic ring fusion in enhancing DNA binding and topoisomerase inhibition. In this context, two distinct intercalative scaffolds were developed by Abbass et al. (2020): a tricyclic [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline-4(5H)-one framework and a bicyclic quinoxaline-2(1H)-one system. These compounds exhibited pronounced antiproliferative activity against HCT-116, HepG2, and MCF-7 cancer cell lines. Importantly, enzymatic evaluation demonstrated effective inhibition of topoisomerase II, with IC50 values ranging from 0.45 to 1.06 μM. Among the tested derivatives, compound 21 emerged as the most potent Topo II inhibitor (IC50=0.45 μM), closely followed by compound 22, underscoring the advantage of increased aromatic fusion in promoting DNA intercalation and enzyme inhibition.

Expansion of triazolo–quinoxaline frameworks has further strengthened the role of this scaffold as a DNA intercalator and topoisomerase II (Topo II) inhibitor. In this context, a series of [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline derivatives reported by El-Adl et al. (2020) were evaluated for antiproliferative activity against HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7 cancer cell lines. Among the twenty-four synthesized derivatives, compounds 8a, 8b, 8c, 8e, 10a, and 11d emerged as the most active Topo II inhibitors, exhibiting IC50 values ranging from 0.379 to 0.813 μM—surpassing the reference drug doxorubicin (IC50=0.94 μM). Notably, compounds 10a and 8e demonstrated the highest potency, which was attributed to favorable hydrophobic and electronic features. In particular, the presence of a distal cyclohexyl moiety linked via a semicarbazide linker in compound 10a, as well as the incorporation of a diethylamine group in compound 8e, significantly enhanced Topo II inhibitory activity, yielding IC50 values of 0.379 and 0.384 μM, respectively. Collectively, these findings emphasize the importance of hydrophobic substituents and linker optimization in improving DNA intercalation and Topo II inhibition within triazolo–quinoxaline derivatives.

Planar acenaphthoquinoxaline frameworks have attracted considerable interest as DNA-intercalating anticancer agents due to their rigid, disc-like architecture and strong π–π stacking capability. In this context, 9-arylacenaphtho[1,2-b]quinoxaline analogues reported by Babu and Paira (2021) were designed to combine therapeutic and imaging potential within a single scaffold. The fused quinoxaline–acenaphthene core confers high molecular planarity, facilitating efficient intercalation into helical DNA and contributing to pronounced antiproliferative activity. Across the synthesized series, the compounds exhibited IC50 values ranging from 2 to 75 μM against multiple cancer cell lines. Notably, compound 5a emerged as the most potent derivative, displaying IC50 values of 1.97 ± 1.29 μM against HeLa cells, 3.06 ± 1.07 μM against MCF-7 cells, and 22.01 ± 0.77 μM against U87MG cells. Importantly, compound 5a also demonstrated favorable selectivity toward cancer cells relative to normal human embryonic kidney (HEK-293) cells, underscoring the potential of acenaphthoquinoxaline-based DNA intercalators as selective anticancer agents.

Systematic exploration of triazolo–quinoxaline scaffolds has further elucidated their potential as DNA-intercalating agents. In this context, a set of seventeen novel [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline derivatives reported by El-Adl et al. (2021a) were screened to identify candidates with enhanced DNA-binding affinity. Based on initial evaluation, compounds 10c, 10d, 10h, 12a, 12b, and 12d were selected for detailed DNA intercalation studies. Among these, compound 12d exhibited the strongest DNA-binding affinity, with an IC50 value of 35.33 ± 1.8 μM, comparable to the reference intercalator doxorubicin (IC50=31.27 ± 1.8 μM). Compounds 12a and 10c also demonstrated appreciable DNA intercalation potency, yielding IC50 values of 39.35 ± 3.9 μM and 42.35 ± 3.9 μM, respectively. Collectively, these findings highlight the importance of substitution patterns within the triazolo–quinoxaline framework in modulating DNA-binding efficiency and reinforce its relevance as a platform for the development of DNA-targeted anticancer agents.

Benzo[g]quinoxaline frameworks with extended aromaticity have also demonstrated notable potential as DNA-intercalating topoisomerase inhibitors. In this context, a series of 2,4-disubstituted benzo[g]quinoxaline derivatives reported by Zaki et al. (2021) were evaluated for their cytotoxic activity against MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Among these, compound 3 emerged as a potent Topoisomerase IIβ (Topo IIβ) inhibitor, achieving an IC50 value of 2.89 ± 0.11 μM, comparable to the reference drug doxorubicin. Mechanistically, the planar and polycyclic architecture of compound 3 facilitates efficient DNA intercalation, thereby disrupting DNA replication and transcription processes. These findings underscore the importance of scaffold planarity and aromatic surface area in enhancing DNA-targeted cytotoxicity within benzo[g]quinoxaline-based anticancer agents.

Metal coordination has also been exploited to enhance the DNA-binding properties of quinoxaline-based systems. In this context, palladium(II)–quinoxaline complexes reported by Dhaduk et al. (2022) were evaluated for their interaction with calf thymus DNA (CT-DNA) and selected proteins using UV–Vis spectroscopy, viscosity measurements, and molecular docking analyses. The combined experimental and computational data consistently supported an intercalative mode of DNA binding. Notably, increasing concentrations of CT-DNA induced pronounced hypochromism at 380 nm accompanied by a slight bathochromic shift, characteristic spectral features associated with quinoxaline ring intercalation between DNA base pairs. These findings highlight the capacity of palladium coordination to reinforce DNA intercalation and stabilize quinoxaline–DNA interactions, further broadening the scope of quinoxaline-based DNA-targeted anticancer agents.

Structure-based investigations have further clarified the interaction of quinoxaline derivatives with topoisomerase IIβ (Topo IIβ) targets. In this context, oxiranyl–quinoxaline derivatives reported by Montero et al. (2022) demonstrated strong binding affinity toward the 3QX3 protein, corresponding to the crystal structure of a Topo IIβ fragment. Molecular interaction analyses revealed that these derivatives closely mimic the binding profile of the known Topo II inhibitor XK-469, predominantly engaging key residues within the winged helix domain (WHD) of Topo IIβ, thereby suggesting a shared inhibitory mechanism. Among the evaluated compounds, 11a exhibited superior cytotoxic potency, with IC50 values of 2.49 ± 1.3 μM against the SK-N-SH human neuroblastoma cell line and 3.96 ± 2.03 μM against IMR-32 cells. Compound 11b also displayed notable activity, yielding IC50 values of 5.3 ± 2.1 μM and 7.1 ± 1.6 μM against SK-N-SH and IMR-32 cells, respectively. Importantly, both 11a and 11b outperformed the reference inhibitor XK-469, which showed IC50 values of 4.6 ± 1.0 μM (SK-N-SH) and 13.0 ± 2.9 μM (IMR-32). Collectively, these findings highlight oxiranyl–quinoxaline derivatives as promising Topo IIβ-targeted anticancer candidates with enhanced cellular efficacy.

Further development of triazolo–quinoxaline frameworks has reinforced their role as DNA-intercalating topoisomerase II (Topo II) inhibitors. In this context, a series of sixteen [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline derivatives reported by Elwan et al. (2022) were designed and synthesized, and their anticancer activity was evaluated against HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7 cell lines. Among the tested models, MCF-7 cells exhibited the highest sensitivity to these derivatives. Compounds 7e, 7c, and 7b emerged as the most active candidates against HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7 cells, respectively. Compound 7e displayed IC50 values of 6.15, 5.75, and 3.41 mM against HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7 cells, respectively, while compound 7c exhibited IC50 values of 6.33, 6.22, and 4.45 mM. Similarly, compound 7b showed IC50 values of 7.46, 6.90, and 5.88 mM across the same cell lines. Notably, these compounds demonstrated higher antiproliferative activity than the reference drug doxorubicin, which exhibited IC50 values of 7.94, 8.07, and 6.75 mM against HepG2, HCT-116, and MCF-7 cells, respectively. Collectively, these findings support the contribution of triazolo–quinoxaline scaffolds to DNA intercalation and Topo II inhibition, with measurable anticancer effects across multiple tumor models.

Structural diversification of quinoxaline derivatives through incorporation of morpholine-, piperidine-, and N-substituted piperazine moieties has further expanded their DNA-targeted anticancer potential. In this context, a series of 2-(quinoxalin-2-yl)-3-arylquinoxaline derivatives reported by Mamedov et al. (2022) demonstrated pronounced cytotoxic activity, particularly when substitution occurred at the 2 or 6 positions of the benzimidazole ring. Mechanistic investigations revealed that these compounds formed stable complexes with nucleic acids, leading to extensive DNA damage and disruption of critical nuclear processes. Their anticancer activity was attributed to a multifaceted mode of action involving DNA intercalation, topoisomerase poisoning, telomerase inhibition, and suppression of gene transcription. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of strategic heterocycle substitution in enhancing DNA binding affinity and multi-target interference with cancer cell proliferation.

Targeted substitution at the 2-position of the quinoxaline scaffold has been shown to enhance antiproliferative activity and multi-target enzyme inhibition in breast cancer models. In this context, a series of novel 2-substituted quinoxaline analogues reported by Salem et al. (2023) demonstrated notable anticancer potential against MCF-7 breast cancer cells. Among the evaluated derivatives, compound 3b emerged as the most active candidate, exhibiting substantial suppression of topoisomerase enzyme activity and potent growth inhibition of MCF-7 cells, with an IC50 value of 1.85 ± 0.11 mM. Molecular modeling studies further supported the therapeutic relevance of compound 3b, revealing strong binding affinity toward the active sites of both topoisomerase II and EGFR proteins. Collectively, these findings suggest that 2-substituted quinoxaline analogues, particularly compound 3b, represent promising dual-target candidates for the development of effective anti-breast cancer agents.

Quinoxaline-based derivatives have also demonstrated selective anticancer activity mediated through topoisomerase II (Topo II) inhibition and apoptosis induction. In this context, a series of quinoxaline analogues reported by Elsakka et al. (2025) were evaluated for their cytotoxic activity against HepG2 and PC-3 cancer cell lines, alongside normal Vero cells, using the MTT assay. Among the tested compounds (I–IV), compounds III and IV exhibited pronounced Topo II inhibitory activity, achieving IC50 values of 21.98 μM and 7.529 μM, respectively, relative to the reference drug doxorubicin. Notably, these compounds induced apoptosis selectively in PC-3 prostate cancer cells, supporting a mechanism of action linked to Topo II inhibition. Collectively, these findings highlight the potential of optimized quinoxaline scaffolds, particularly compound IV, as selective Topo II–targeted anticancer agents with apoptosis-inducing capability.

Targeting both DNA topology and oncogene regulation has emerged as a promising anticancer strategy. In this context, a series of dibenzoquinoxaline derivatives reported by Hu and Lin (2021) were evaluated for their dual ability to inhibit topoisomerase I (Topo I) and stabilize the c-MYC G-quadruplex (G4) structure. Among the synthesized compounds, 5 emerged as the most promising dual-acting ligand, demonstrating effective inhibition of Topo I activity alongside pronounced stabilization of the c-MYC G4 motif. This dual mechanism highlights the capacity of dibenzoquinoxaline scaffolds to simultaneously disrupt DNA relaxation processes and suppress oncogene transcription, reinforcing their potential as multifunctional anticancer agents.

Metal-based quinoxaline complexes have further expanded the scope of DNA-targeted anticancer strategies through alternative binding modes. In this context, bishomoleptic and trisheteroleptic ruthenium–diimine complexes bearing 2-(2-pyridyl)quinoxaline ligands, reported by Balou et al. (2021), were investigated for their interactions with calf thymus DNA (CT-DNA) and anticancer activity. Molecular docking studies confirmed that complexes 1 and 2 interact with DNA primarily through minor groove binding, supported by sequence-specific binding profiles. Biological evaluation using MTT assays revealed that both complexes effectively induced apoptosis in MCF-7 breast cancer cells at low concentrations. Notably, complex 2exhibited enhanced cellular uptake and preferential nuclear localization in MCF-7 cells compared with non-cancerous HEK-293 cells, highlighting its improved selectivity and intracellular targeting. Collectively, these findings underscore the potential of ruthenium–quinoxaline complexes as selective DNA-binding agents capable of inducing apoptosis in breast cancer cells.

The current data collectively indicate that DNA intercalation and Topo II inhibition remain central mechanisms for quinoxaline derivatives, with planar fused systems (acenaphthoquinoxalines, triazolo-quinoxalines) showing particularly high potency. SAR analysis indicates that rigid aromatic scaffolds and hydrophobic substituents enhance intercalation, while polar groups improve solubility and selectivity. The strongest activities are seen in MCF-7, HepG2, and HeLa cells, suggesting utility in breast and liver cancers. Notably, several derivatives match or exceed doxorubicin in Topo II inhibition, underscoring their therapeutic promise. Nonetheless, DNA intercalators raise concerns about genotoxicity and off-target toxicity, which have been insufficiently addressed in current studies. Future research should focus on selectivity, in vivo safety assessment, and the design of hybrid molecules that balance potency with reduced systemic toxicity.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as tubulin polymerization inhibitors
sec.p: Disruption of microtubule dynamics represents a validated anticancer strategy, as precise regulation of tubulin polymerization and depolymerization is essential for mitotic spindle formation, cell division, and cell migration (McLoughlin and O’Boyle, 2020). Tubulin polymerization inhibitors exert their antitumor effects primarily by binding to the colchicine-binding site (CBS) on β-tubulin, thereby preventing microtubule assembly, inducing G2/M cell cycle arrest, and ultimately triggering apoptosis or necrosis (McLoughlin and O’Boyle, 2020). Within this context, quinoxaline-based scaffolds have emerged as promising tubulin-targeting agents, owing to their planar heteroaromatic structure, which facilitates effective interaction with the CBS pocket. Recent studies have demonstrated that several quinoxaline derivatives exhibit potent antiproliferative activity through inhibition of tubulin polymerization, highlighting this scaffold as a versatile platform for the development of microtubule-disrupting anticancer agents (Goel et al., 2023).

Quinoxaline derivatives targeting the colchicine-binding site (CBS) on tubulin have demonstrated promising microtubule-disrupting activity. In this context, compound 1A2, reported by Goel et al. (2023), emerged as a representative example of a colchicine-like tubulin polymerization inhibitor, exhibiting strong binding affinity within the CBS of the tubulin protein. This interaction translated into notable cytotoxic activity against multiple cancer cell lines, including MCF-7, MDA-MB-231, HCT-116, and A549, with IC50 values of 4.33 ± 0.31, 6.11 ± 0.23, 5.87 ± 0.31, and 5.44 ± 0.18 μM, respectively. In addition to 1A2, related derivatives (1E3, 1E7, 1E8, 1E12, and 1E13) also exhibited strong tubulin-binding affinity and effective inhibition of tubulin polymerization. Collectively, these findings highlight the ability of CBS-targeting quinoxaline derivatives to disrupt microtubule dynamics, leading to growth inhibition and cell death in cancer cells, and reinforce their potential as tubulin-targeted anticancer agents.

Further evidence supporting the role of quinoxaline derivatives as tubulin polymerization inhibitors was provided by Ommi et al. (2023). In this study, compound 5l exhibited pronounced cytotoxic activity against A549 lung cancer cells, with an IC50 value of 4.37 ± 0.09 μM. Structure-based analysis revealed that 5lbinds strongly to the colchicine-binding site of α/β-tubulin, achieving a binding free energy of −45.139 kcal/mol. This high binding affinity was consistent with its potent inhibition of tubulin polymerization, with an IC50 value below 2.19 μM. The combined cellular and mechanistic data indicate that disruption of microtubule dynamics underlies the anticancer activity of 5l, reinforcing the potential of CBS-targeting quinoxaline derivatives as effective microtubule-disrupting anticancer agents.

Quinoxaline derivatives have also demonstrated exceptional potency as tubulin polymerization inhibitors through effective targeting of the colchicine-binding site (CBS). In this context, compounds 11a and 11b, reported by Liang et al. (2021), emerged as the most potent antiproliferative agents within their series. Notably, compound 11a exhibited sub-micromolar cytotoxicity, with IC50 values of 0.16 ± 0.02 μM against HeLa cells and 0.18 ± 0.03 μM against HT-29 cells. Mechanistic investigations revealed that 11a inhibited tubulin polymerization in a dose-dependent manner, leading to cell cycle arrest at the G2/M phase and subsequent induction of apoptosis. Molecular docking studies further confirmed strong binding of 11a within the colchicine-binding pocket of tubulin, providing a structural basis for its potent microtubule-disrupting activity. Collectively, these findings highlight compound 11a as a highly efficient tubulin polymerization inhibitor with significant anticancer potential.

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline derivatives acting on the colchicine-binding site of tubulin demonstrate potent antiproliferative activity, with IC50 values in the sub-micromolar range for certain analogs. SAR evaluation highlights the importance of bulky substituents and halogen groups in enhancing tubulin binding and inducing G2/M arrest. Activity has been reported across multiple cancers, including breast, lung, and colorectal models, indicating broad applicability. Compared to classical tubulin inhibitors, quinoxaline-based molecules may offer structural novelty that could reduce cross-resistance. However, current evidence is mainly limited to docking and in vitro polymerization assays, with scarce in vivo validation. Future studies should prioritize pharmacological characterization in animal tumor models, along with structural refinements to enhance metabolic stability and minimize neurotoxicity.

sec.title: Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS)
sec.p: Quinoxaline derivatives as ROS Generation: ROS are chemically reactive molecules that include oxygen, such as peroxides, superoxide, hydroxyl radicals, and singlet oxygen (Juan et al., 2021). These species are natural byproducts of cellular metabolism that serve important roles in cell signaling and homeostasis (Juan et al., 2021). However, excessive ROS production can harm cellular components, including DNA, proteins, and lipids, causing oxidative stress and cancer formation (Nakamura and Takada, 2021).

One study by Fan et al. (2022) focuses on the compounds of quinoxaline and arylfuran, namely QW12 Using an IC50 value of 10.58 µM against HeLa cells, QW12 has been found to be an effective anticancer drug. Through ROS production and cell cycle arrest, QW12 causes apoptosis in cancerous cells. Its efficacy has been proven in several cancer cell lines, such as HeLa cells, where it prevents the phosphorylation of Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3), a crucial signaling pathway in cancer development.

Further study by Varma et al. (2021) demonstrated that quinoxaline derivatives, particularly those synthesized as rhenium(I) carbonyl complexes, have shown significant promise in targeting ROS in cancer cells. Notably, complexes (L1–L5) exhibited significant anticancer activity, with IC50 values of 13.94 μg/mL (L1), 12.12 μg/mL (L2), 12.10 μg/mL (L3), 12.05 μg/mL (L4), and 9.85 μg/mL (L5). These compounds, characterized by their unique ligand structures, were shown to elevate ROS levels, especially hydrogen peroxide, leading to apoptosis induction and inhibition of cancer cell proliferation through ROS modulation.

Finally, a study by Sibiya (2020) demonstrated that the quinoxaline derivatives LA-39B and LA-55 were ultimately shown to be the most efficacious in regulating the levels of ROS in cancerous cells. It has been demonstrated that LA-39B and LA-55 raise intracellular ROS levels in cancer cells, such as A549 lung cancer cells, which may be responsible for some of their anticancer properties with IC50 values of 46.97 μM and 51.91 μM respectively, at 25 μM concentration. The increased ROS produced by these quinoxaline derivatives eventually activated the cancer cells’ apoptotic cell death pathways, which also caused oxidative stress and DNA damage. However, this compound showed preferential toxicity towards cancer cells in non-cancerous cells such as Raw 264.7 macrophages, which showed antioxidant qualities and decreased ROS levels.

The collective evidence indicates that quinoxaline derivatives capable of elevating intracellular ROS commonly feature electron-withdrawing substituents such as chloro or fluoro groups, or fused heteroaromatic rings that enhance redox cycling and mitochondrial destabilization. SAR trends highlight that conjugation with imidazole or benzimidazole moieties promotes ROS generation and downstream caspase activation, while alkyl substitutions on the phenyl ring improve cell penetration and potency. Activity profiles show particularly strong effects in hepatocellular (HepG2) and breast (MCF-7) cancer cells, though prostate and colorectal lines also respond, suggesting a broad multi-target oxidative mechanism. Despite these advances, most reports remain limited to in-vitro assays and rarely quantify antioxidant defense disruption or in-vivo oxidative stress, leaving unanswered questions regarding selectivity and systemic safety. Future studies should incorporate animal models to assess redox balance, explore combination therapy with antioxidant modulators, and refine structural motifs to maximize tumor specificity while minimizing off-target oxidative damage.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as c-met inhibitors
sec.p: c-Met is a prototype member of a subfamily of heterodimeric receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) and is the receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) (Bottaro et al., 1991). Binding of HGF to its receptor c-Met induces several complexes signaling pathways that result in cell proliferation, survival, motility, induction of cell polarity, scattering, angiogenesis, and invasion (Parikh and Ghate, 2018). Blocking c-Met kinase activity with small-molecule inhibitors has been identified as a promising approach for cancer treatment.

A series of 4-phenoxypyridine-based 3-oxo-3,4-dihydroquinoxaline derivatives were biologically evaluated by Wang et al. (2020b) as c-Met kinase inhibitors. The evaluation of inhibitory activities against c-Met kinase indicated that most compounds showed excellent c-Met kinase activity in vitro, with IC50 values of ten compounds (23a, 23e, 23f, 23l, 23r, 23s, 23v, 23w, 23x, and 23y) being less than 10 nM. Notably, three of them, compound 23v, 23w, and 23y demonstrated remarkable potency with IC50 values of 2.31 nM, 1.91 nM, and 2.44 nM, respectively, exceeding the potency of the positive control drug foretinib (c-Met, IC50=2.53 nM).

Another in vitro study conducted by Ahamed et al. (2022) on novel quinoxaline derivatives (DPQC) and (MDBD) showed significant in vitro anticancer activity. Hence, these compounds were further investigated in silico molecular docking analysis against the 3F66 (c-Met-kinase; a hepatocyte growth factor) protein target. The auto dock software provided superior results for the title compound MDBD, which exhibited a higher ligand-receptor interaction energy value of -10.8 (kcal/mol) against 3F66 protein and a 0.01187 µM inhibition constant (ki) with (active site A) presented amino acids such as A: ARG1086, A: MET1211, A: VAL1092, A: ALA1226, A: ALA1108, A: MET1211.

The collective evidence indicates that quinoxaline-based c-Met inhibitors achieve their potency through key structural motifs, notably a 4-fluorophenoxy group, a free piperazine or methylpiperazine moiety, and additional halogen substitutions on the quinoxaline core, all of which enhance c-Met kinase binding and downstream Akt pathway suppression. Comparative analyses reveal strong antiproliferative effects in triple-negative breast (MDA-MB-231) and colorectal (HT-29) cancer cells, and several compounds display dual inhibition of c-Met and related kinases such as EGFR, highlighting multi-target potential. SAR trends further suggest that the quinoxaline aryl-ether scaffold and flexible linkers contribute to both binding affinity and favorable pharmacokinetic properties. Nevertheless, current research remains largely limited to in-vitro studies, with minimal exploration of resistance mechanisms or in-vivo pharmacokinetics. Future work should incorporate comprehensive kinase selectivity profiling, animal efficacy models, and structural optimization to advance these promising leads toward clinical application.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as PARP inhibitors
sec.p: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors are an important class of drugs that target the PARP enzyme, which is crucial for DNA repair.
