By blocking PARP, these inhibitors cause the accumulation of DNA damage in cancer cells, resulting in cell death, especially in cells deficient in other DNA repair mechanisms. This mechanism makes PARP inhibitors a valuable option in cancer treatment.

In a study by Syam et al. (2022) the PARP-1 inhibitory activity of new quinoxaline compounds was assessed using a colorimetric 96-well assay. The IC50 values, representing the concentration needed to inhibit PARP-1 by 50%, ranged from 2.31 to 57.35 nM, with Olaparib as the reference drug. Notably, quinoxaline derivatives demonstrated a promising impact on PARP-1 suppression, particularly compound 8a which exhibited nearly 2-fold higher potency with an IC50 of 2.31 nM compared to Olaparib’s IC50 of 4.40 nM. The study highlighted that the structure-activity relationship (SAR) of these quinoxaline derivatives plays a critical role in their efficacy, with hydrophobic residues in the compounds being associated with increased inhibitory activity. These results suggest that quinoxaline derivatives have strong potential as effective PARP-1 inhibitors and could be promising candidates for cancer therapy.

In a related study by Thabet et al. (2022) the PARP-1 and EGFR inhibitory activities of quinoxaline derivatives were evaluated. Among the compounds tested, compound 8i exhibited the most promising dual enzyme inhibition. It showed a PARP-1 IC50 value of 1.37 nM, compared to olaparib’s 1.49 nM, and an EGFR IC50 value of 64.65 nM, compared to erlotinib’s 80 nM. Notably, erlotinib and lynparza are FDA-approved and marketed under the trade names tarceva and lynparza, respectively. Compound 8i also demonstrated high cytotoxic activity with IC50 values of 0.12 μM and 1.31 μM against MDA-MB-231 and MCF-7 cells, respectively. Additionally, it induced apoptosis in MDA-MB 231 cells by 38-fold, arrested the cell cycle at the G2/M phase, and affected apoptosis-related genes. Virtual binding studies revealed that compound 8i had favorable interactions with PARP-1 and EGFR proteins, highlighting its potential as a dual-target anti-breast cancer agent. The findings underscore the effectiveness of quinoxaline derivatives in targeting PARP-1, reinforcing their potential as valuable candidates in cancer treatment.

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline derivatives exhibit strong potential as PARP-1 inhibitors, with SAR analyses highlighting the role of hydrophobic substitutions in enhancing inhibitory potency. Bis-triazolothiadiazine derivatives demonstrated superior activity compared to the reference drug Olaparib, underscoring the suitability of the quinoxaline scaffold for further optimization of PARP-1 binding affinity. A noteworthy observation is the trend toward dual-target inhibition, as certain bis-triazolothiadiazine derivatives exhibited activity against both PARP-1 and EGFR, suggesting a promising strategy to overcome resistance associated with single-target PARP inhibitors. Despite these encouraging findings, most investigations remain limited to in vitro enzyme inhibition and cytotoxicity assays, with insufficient evaluation of selectivity, pharmacokinetics, or in vivo efficacy. Future studies should prioritize evaluating the in vivo efficacy and pharmacokinetic properties of quinoxaline-based PARP inhibitors, investigate their ability to overcome resistance to existing therapies, and explore the therapeutic relevance of dual-target inhibition as a strategy to achieve broader and more durable anticancer effects.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as inhibition of proliferation pathways
sec.p: Inhibitors of proliferation pathways can work through various mechanisms, such as blocking growth factor receptors, interfering with downstream signaling molecules, or disrupting cell cycle progression (Montero et al., 2022). Examples include tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, and CDK inhibitors.

A study by Ward et al. (2024) focuses on compound 15 derived from 4-oxotriazoloquinoxaline, showed the highest potency as an antiproliferative agent compared to other synthesized quinoxaline derivatives. It showed significant cytotoxicity against various human cancer cell types, with IC50 values of 9.81 ± 0.7 μM for liver cancer (HepG2), 15.49 ± 1.2 μM for PC3 cell line, and 10.09 ± 0.9 μM for MCF-7 cell line. The effectiveness of the standard chemotherapy drug doxorubicin, with IC50 values of 14.61 ± 1.1 μM, 16.32 ± 1.1 μM, and 12.41 ± 0.74 μM against the same cell lines, was outperformed by these results.

In another study by Aboelmagd et al. (2020) synthesized and evaluated 35 N-pentylquinoxaline carboxamides and their O-regioisomers to assess their antiproliferative activity. Among these, 14 compounds exhibited significant inhibitory effects on HCT-116 cancer cells, with compound 14b showing the highest potency, recording an IC50 value of 0.43 ± 0.08 mM. SAR analysis revealed that various side chains, including natural and unnatural amino acids and non-amino acid derivatives, were generally well-tolerated. Interestingly, leucine derivatives exhibited superior activity, particularly in the O-substituted regioisomer 13d compared to the N-substituted isomer 10d. Moreover, compounds such as 9f, 14b, 12b, and 9g significantly increased caspase-3 activity in HCT-116 cells, indicating that the observed cell death was likely due to apoptosis. This was further corroborated by DAPI staining, which confirmed nuclear disintegration and morphological changes in the treated cancer cells, such as nuclear condensation and membrane alteration. Notably, the study also demonstrated that these compounds did not exhibit cytotoxicity against normal HEK-293 cells, highlighting their selectivity for cancerous cells and underscoring their potential as targeted cancer therapeutics.

Recent findings highlight that quinoxaline derivatives demonstrate significant potential as antiproliferative agents by effectively disrupting critical signaling pathways and inducing apoptosis in cancer cells. Compounds such as the 4-oxotriazoloquinoxaline derivative (compound 15) have shown superior cytotoxicity compared to standard chemotherapy drugs like doxorubicin across multiple cancer cell lines, underscoring their therapeutic promise. Similarly, N-pentylquinoxaline carboxamides and their O-regioisomers exhibited strong selectivity toward malignant cells while sparing normal counterparts, suggesting a favorable therapeutic index. The mechanistic evidence, including caspase-3 activation and nuclear disintegration, further supports apoptosis as a central mode of action. Collectively, these findings underscore the versatility of quinoxaline scaffolds in targeting proliferation pathways and highlight their potential for development into selective anticancer therapeutics.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as cytotoxic activity
sec.p: Cytotoxic anticancer medications work by interfering with vital cellular functions to either stop the development of cancer cells or cause them to die. Targeting rapidly dividing cells, these medications frequently interfere with RNA production, cell division, or DNA replication.

One of the studies by Guillon et al. (2020) assessed the cytotoxic action of 1-phenyl-8-[[4-(pyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxaline-4-yl)phenyl]methyl].-1,3,8-triazaspiro[4.5]decan-4-one was evaluated using the MTS test on human leukemia cell lines the K562, U937, and HL60. This compound demonstrated considerable antiproliferative action against the K562 chronic myeloid leukemia cell line, with an IC50 of 3.5 μM, outperforming the reference drug A6730 (IC50=17 μM). It also showed lower activity against the HL60 acute myeloblastic leukemia cell line, with an IC50 of 15 μM compared to A6730 (IC50=5.5 μM). The same compound was ineffective against the U937 myeloblastic cell line (IC50 >20 μM). Moreover, it showed less cytotoxicity against normal T-lymphocytes (PBMNC + PHA) with an IC50 above 35.0 μM, suggesting probable selectivity towards cancer cells, namely K562 (selectivity index=10).

Another study by Guillon et al. (2022) focuses on the newly synthesized pyrroloquinoxaline compound 9’s toxicity efficiency was appraised against leukemia cell lines K562, U937, and HL60 using the MTS assay. Exposure to this Compound led to moderate Leukemic inhibition of the K562 cell line, and the calculated IC50 of 17 μM was found to be pretty much equal when compared to the reference Compound A6730 (IC50=17 μM) and a bit better than the other Compound JG576 (IC50=19 μm). On the other hand, against the HL60 acute human myeloblastic leukemia cell line, Compound 9 just marked a lower IC50 of 31 μM, which is much higher than A6730’s IC50=5.5 μM. Nonetheless, compound 9 exhibited the best performance in U937 cells with an IC50 of 8 μM, which was the same as A6730 and better than JG576 (IC50=12 μM). The current data reveals that the new pyrroloquinoxaline derivative 9 is a promising compound with cytotoxic potential against human leukemia cell lines, the IC50 s being under 31 μM.

Current findings collectively demonstrate that pyrroloquinoxaline derivatives exhibit significant cytotoxic potential against leukemia cell lines, with some compounds outperforming reference drugs and showing favorable selectivity toward cancer cells. Activity varies across cell lines, with the greatest efficacy observed in K562 and U937 cells. While these results highlight the promise of quinoxaline scaffolds for hematologic malignancies, evidence is limited to in vitro studies, and mechanisms of cell death remain incompletely characterized. Future studies should include in vivo validation, detailed exploration of apoptotic versus non-apoptotic pathways, and structure optimization to enhance potency and selectivity across diverse cancer types.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as PFKFB3 kinase inhibitors
sec.p: PFKFB3 kinase is vital in regulating glycolysis by synthesizing fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which activates phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1), a key enzyme in glycolysis (Kotowski et al., 2021). This is especially important in cancer cells that depend on glycolysis for energy (the Warburg effect) (Wang et al., 2020a). Inhibiting PFKFB3 disrupts cancer cell metabolism, reducing their growth and proliferation (Wang et al., 2020a).

A study by Abad et al. (2023) characterized a novel triazolequinoxalin (TZQ) derivative, designated as compound 4 using various spectroscopic methods and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The structure crystallizes in the monoclinic space group C2/c, stabilized by intermolecular interactions, which were evaluated through Hirshfeld surface analysis and a 2D chemical fingerprints map. Molecular docking studies predicted compound 4 exhibits significant hydrophilic and hydrophobic interactions at the PFKFB3 kinase active site; this suggests that compound 4 is a promising candidate for further investigation as an effective inhibitor of PFKFB3 kinase in cancer therapy.

Current data indicate that TZQ derivatives are promising PFKFB3 inhibitors, capable of disrupting glycolysis and cancer cell proliferation. Structural analyses and molecular docking suggest strong binding to the PFKFB3 active site, but functional validation in enzymatic, cellular, and in vivo models is still lacking. Future studies should confirm kinase inhibition, assess metabolic effects, and optimize SAR to establish selective and effective anticancer activity.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as PTP1B inhibitors
sec.p: Quinoxaline derivatives, particularly pyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxalines, have shown promise as PTP1B inhibitors. This is significant given PTP1B’s dual role in cancer as a tumour suppressor/promoter and its involvement in immune signalling. Based on enzyme kinetics and computational calculations, a variety of compounds have been reported to selectively inhibit PTP1B by targeting the α3/α6/α7 tunnel (Sánchez-Alonso et al., 2021).

A recent study done by Sánchez-Alonso et al. (2021) has demonstrated that pyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxalines act as selective PTP1B inhibitors through an allosteric mechanism, targeting the α3/α6/α7 tunnel, as supported by computational methods. These inhibitors mimic insulin in cellular by enhancing glucose uptake and phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate (IRS). Furthermore, pyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxal-5-inium salts and 4,5-dihydropyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxalines have been identified as new PTP1B inhibitors with similar insulin-mimetic effects. Molecular docking studies of these inhibitors at the α3/α6/α7 tunnel have been conducted. The inhibitory activity of these compounds was screened using a colorimetric malachite green assay with human recombinant PTP1B and insulin receptor substrate 5 (IR5), showing inhibitory activities between 22% and 56% at 1 μM, with compounds 3 generally being more active than compound 2.

Current findings indicate that pyrrolo[1,2-a]quinoxaline derivatives selectively inhibit PTP1B through an allosteric mechanism at the α3/α6/α7 tunnel, enhancing insulin-like signaling and supporting their dual relevance in cancer and metabolic regulation. While these scaffolds show moderate inhibitory activity and favorable docking profiles, evidence is limited to enzymatic and computational assays. Further studies should validate their effects in cancer models, clarify the context dependent role of PTP1B, and optimize structures for greater potency and selectivity.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as dual MMP-9/MAO-A inhibitors
sec.p: MMP-9, a zinc-dependent endopeptidase, is a potential therapeutic target for halting colorectal cancer (CRC) metastasis (Buhmeida et al., 2009). Additionally, monoamine oxidases (MAOs), particularly MAO-A, have been implicated in CRC progression and metastasis by promoting epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) (Aljanabi et al., 2021). Combining the structural features of MMP-9 and MAO-A inhibitors, novel dual inhibitors have been designed by Ayoup et al. (2021) using a 3-benzyl quinoxaline scaffold. These were decorated with selected zinc-binding groups (ZBGs) and pharmacophoric moieties to enhance MMP-9 inhibition while maintaining MAO-A inhibition. Compounds (8), (16), (17), (19), and (28) showed higher MMP-9 inhibition than quercetin, with compound 19 being the most potent (IC50=4.50 nM). Additionally, these compounds were more active than reference MAO inhibitors, with compounds 16 and 19 showing the highest activity against MAO-A and compound 19 being the most selective MAO-A inhibitor.

Emerging results support that 3-benzyl quinoxaline scaffolds can function as dual MMP-9 and MAO-A inhibitors, targeting key pathways involved in colorectal cancer progression and metastasis. Structural optimization with zinc-binding groups has yielded compounds with greater potency than quercetin for MMP-9 inhibition and superior activity compared to reference MAO inhibitors, with some derivatives showing strong selectivity for MAO-A. While these findings highlight the therapeutic promise of dual inhibition, current studies remain limited to in vitro assays. Future work should validate efficacy in colorectal cancer models, assess pharmacokinetics and safety, and explore whether dual-targeting strategies can effectively reduce metastasis in vivo.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as BRD9 inhibitors
sec.p: Detailed SAR studies highlighted the crucial role of substituents at the C-1 and C-4 positions in enhancing selectivity and binding affinity. This led to the discovery of a second-generation BRD9 binder (Bromodomain-containing protein 9) is a member of the bromodomain and extra terminal (BET) family of proteins that significantly recognize acetylated lysine residues on histones. It influences gene expression and chromatin remodeling, which are crucial processes in cancer development.

A study by Gazzillo et al. (2023) focuses on designing, synthesizing, and evaluating [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline-based compounds as potential BRD9 inhibitors. New derivatives were created by modifying the linker at the C-4 position and exploring different alkyl substituents at the C-1 position, resulting in 16 new compounds synthesized via Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling. The importance of the amine spacer at the C-4 position for effective BRD9 binding was highlighted. Compounds 24 and 36 demonstrated excellent selectivity towards BRD9 and significant antiproliferative effects on leukemia cell lines, particularly CCRF-CEM, without cytotoxicity to healthy cells. These compounds are also bound with BRPF1, suggesting potential as dual inhibitors. An updated pharmacophore model, “pharm-druglike2.1,” was developed to improve BRD9 selectivity by incorporating a hydrogen bond donor feature for interaction with the Ile53 residue. In vitro assays confirmed the anticancer activity of compounds 24 and 36 with IC50 values below 100 µM across various leukemia cell lines.

Recent studies highlight that triazoloquinoxaline-based scaffolds can serve as selective BRD9 inhibitors by exploiting key substituent modifications at the C-1 and C-4 positions. Optimized derivatives demonstrated strong BRD9 binding, significant antiproliferative effects in leukemia cell lines, and minimal toxicity toward normal cells. Importantly, some compounds also displayed dual binding to BRPF1, suggesting potential for broader epigenetic modulation. While these results emphasize the promise of quinoxaline derivatives as BRD9-targeting agents, limitations include the reliance on in vitro assays and the absence of in vivo efficacy or safety data. Future research should focus on validating these inhibitors in animal models, assessing pharmacokinetics, and clarifying whether dual BRD9/BRPF1 activity enhances therapeutic benefit or introduces selectivity challenges.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as a BD1-selective BET
sec.p: ε-N-Acetylation of lysine residues (Kac) is crucial in biological processes such as chromatin remodeling and regulation of transcription factors (Choudhary et al., 2009). Bromodomains, particularly those in the BET family (BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT), recognize Kac and are key targets for small-molecule inhibitors due to their roles in cell cycle regulation and cancer progression (Filippakopoulos and Knapp, 2014).

This study was done by Ali et al. (2024) on BET inhibitors DW-71177, an orally bioavailable, BD1-selective BET inhibitor with 10-20-fold higher selectivity for BD1 over BD2. DW-71177 demonstrated promising in vivo efficacy in a mouse model of AML. When tested for growth-inhibitory activity against various tumor cell lines, DW-71177 exhibited strong growth inhibition (GI50 <1.0 μM) in 5 out of 17 cell lines, including NUT midline carcinoma (Ty-82), AML cell lines (MV4-11, THP-1), and B-cell lymphoma lines (Pfeiffer, SU-DHL-4). In contrast, chronic myeloid leukemia (K562) and most solid tumor cell lines were less sensitive. This inhibition profile was similar to that of the pan-BET inhibitor OTX-015.In MV4-11 cells, DW-71177 reduced c-MYC and phosphorylated ERK1/2 levels while increasing p21 expression, similar to OTX-015. It also induced cell cycle arrest in the sub-G1 phase and increased apoptosis (Fig. 4).

The current data collectively indicate that quinoxaline-based BD1-selective BET inhibitors represent a promising avenue for targeted cancer therapy. Compounds such as DW-71177 demonstrated potent sub-micromolar activity, selective inhibition of BRD4-BD1 over BD2, and robust induction of apoptosis across AML, NUT midline carcinoma, and lymphoma cell lines. Mechanistic studies further revealed suppression of c-MYC expression, decreased ERK1/2 phosphorylation, and cell cycle arrest at the sub-G1 phase, underscoring their ability to disrupt oncogenic transcriptional programs. Nevertheless, variability in response across tumor types, limited in vivo studies, and the absence of direct comparisons with pan-BET inhibitors highlight important research gaps. Future investigations should focus on pharmacokinetic optimization, resistance profiling, and rational combination strategies to fully establish the translational potential of BD1-selective inhibitors as safer and more effective alternatives in BET-targeted oncology.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as CK2 inhibitors
sec.p: Casein kinase 2 (CK2) is a serine/threonine protein kinase involved in crucial cellular processes such as cell cycle regulation and DNA repair. Its overexpression in cancers makes CK2 a key target for anticancer drug development. CK2 inhibitors can disrupt these pathways, suppressing tumor growth and proliferation.

A study by Winiewska-Szajewska et al. (2021) evaluated the binding affinities and inhibitory activities of new compounds targeting CK2 using a thermal shift assay (nanoDSF). Among these, quinoxaline derivatives (6a–e) exhibited negligible interaction with CK2, with ΔTm values never exceeding 1°C. However, certain derivatives like 7e demonstrated higher inhibitory activity with micromolar IC50 values, indicating that specific modifications can enhance their potential as CK2 inhibitors in anticancer therapy.

The current data collectively indicate that research on quinoxaline-based CK2 inhibitors is still at an early stage, with only limited experimental evidence available. Among the reported derivatives, most compounds exhibited negligible interaction with CK2, whereas compound 7e showed higher inhibitory activity at the micromolar level, suggesting that appropriate structural modifications can enhance biological efficacy. These preliminary findings highlight the potential of CK2 as a therapeutic target for quinoxaline scaffolds; however, the evidence remains insufficient to establish conclusive trends. Future studies should therefore expand SAR analyses, investigate selectivity against related kinases, and conduct in vivo validation to clarify the translational potential of this emerging class of inhibitors.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as HDAC inhibitors
sec.p: Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACIs) are a class of compounds that inhibit the function of histone deacetylases (HDACs), enzymes responsible for removing acetyl groups from histone proteins. This deacetylation process plays a key role in the regulation of gene expression. By inhibiting HDACs, HDACIs can induce apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, and differentiation in cancer cells, making them promising candidates for cancer therapy.

A study by Ma et al. (2021) involved the synthesis of twenty-seven new quinoxaline derivatives with various substitutions to explore their SAR as potential anticancer agents targeting HDAC enzymes, specifically HDAC1, HDAC4, and HDAC6. Twenty synthesized compounds demonstrated cytotoxic effects ranging from very strong to moderate against two liver cancer cell lines, HepG-2 and HuH-7. The ten most active compounds 6c, 6d, 6f, 6g, 6k, 6l, 7b, 8, 10h, and 12 were further evaluated for their HDAC inhibitory activity. These compounds exhibited IC50 values ranging from 1.39 to 7.21 µM, compared to the reference drug, suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA). Compound 6c showed the most potent cytotoxicity against HepG-2 and HuH-7 cell lines, with IC50 values of 1.53 µM for HepG-2 and 3.06 µM for HuH-7. Additionally, it was the most effective inhibitor of HDAC1, HDAC4, and HDAC6, with IC50 values of 1.76 µM, 1.39 µM, and 3.46 µM, in that order.

The current data collectively indicates that quinoxaline-based HDAC inhibitors demonstrate significant promise as anticancer agents by effectively targeting multiple HDAC isoforms and inducing potent cytotoxic effects in liver cancer cell lines. Structure–activity analyses suggest that specific substitutions, particularly in compounds such as 6c, can markedly improve inhibitory activity, achieving IC₅₀ values in the low micromolar range and showing comparable or superior efficacy to the reference drug SAHA. These results underscore the therapeutic potential of quinoxaline scaffolds as HDAC inhibitors; however, the available studies are restricted to in vitro models and lack in vivo validation or mechanistic exploration of apoptotic pathways. Future research should therefore focus on optimizing SAR features, expanding selectivity profiling across HDAC isoforms, and conducting preclinical evaluations to determine the translational potential of this emerging class.

sec.title: Quinoxaline derivatives as PIM kinase family
sec.p: The PIM kinase family, particularly Pim-1, is vital for cell cycle regulation and cancer progression. Pim-1, a serine-threonine kinase, boosts cell cycle progression by phosphorylating key regulators like Cdc25C (Bachmann et al., 2006). This phosphorylation enhances Cdc25C’s activity at the G2/M transition, facilitating the progression to G1. Pim-1 and Cdc25C co-localize in the cytoplasm, highlighting Pim-1’s role as a positive cell cycle regulator (Bachmann et al., 2006).

A recent study by Oyallon et al. (2021) explored quinoxaline-2-carboxylic acid derivatives as dual inhibitors of these kinases. Using a structure-based design, the researchers modified a lead compound with halogenated groups at the 6-position to enhance its inhibition of Pim-2 (Oyallon et al., 2021). The modified compounds showed improved interaction with a hydrophobic pocket in the Pim kinases, as confirmed by docking studies (Oyallon et al., 2021). Two potent derivatives 5c and 5e exhibited sub-micromolar activity against both Pim-1 and Pim-2. In vitro assays on cancer cell lines overexpressing Pim-1/2 showed effective micromolar growth inhibition. These findings highlight the potential of these quinoxaline derivatives for targeted cancer therapies and warrant further pharmacomodulation studies.

The current evidence indicates that quinoxaline-based derivatives targeting the PIM kinase family hold potential as dual inhibitors of Pim-1 and Pim-2. Compounds such as 5c and 5e demonstrated sub-micromolar activity and effective growth inhibition in cancer cell lines, suggesting that halogen substitution at the 6-position can enhance binding affinity. While these findings highlight the promise of quinoxaline scaffolds for PIM-targeted therapies, further studies are required to validate their efficacy in vivo and to establish their translational relevance in cancer treatment.

sec.title: Inhibition of folate enzymes
sec.p: Quinoxaline derivatives as folate enzyme inhibitors: Folate enzymes are essential for DNA synthesis, repair, and cellular proliferation, making them key targets in cancer therapy (Yang et al., 2021). These enzymes facilitate the conversion of folate into tetrahydrofolate, a critical cofactor in synthesizing nucleotides and amino acids. Disruption in folate metabolism can lead to impaired DNA synthesis and repair, which is particularly impactful in rapidly dividing cancer cells (Yang et al., 2021).

A recent study by El Rayes et al. (2022) investigated the antiproliferative effects of quinoxaline peptidomimetics on various cancer cell lines, focusing on their interactions with folate enzymes. The study tested 27 synthetic compounds using the MTT assay to assess their impact on cancer cell quinoxaline (El Rayes et al., 2022). Among these, fourteen compounds showed significant inhibition of HCT-116 colorectal cancer cells. Compound 10b was identified as the most effective, while compound 9c demonstrated the least activity. In MCF-7 breast cancer cells, fifteen compounds were effective, with compound 10b again showing the highest potency.

Their work revealed that these compounds selectively target cancer cells, showing no cytotoxic effects on normal HEK-293 cells. Molecular docking studies demonstrated that the most active quinoxaline derivatives bind predominantly at the homodimer interface of human thymidylate synthase (hTS), stabilizing its inactive conformation. This binding was achieved through key interactions with residues such as Gln172, Arg175, Ile190, Met191, and Cys192 from chain A and Leu204 and Pro205 from chain B. These interactions inhibit cell growth by stabilizing the inactive form of hTS, suggesting a promising mechanism for targeted cancer therapy.

The current data collectively suggest that quinoxaline-based folate enzyme inhibitors represent a promising class of anticancer agents through selective targeting of thymidylate synthase and disruption of DNA synthesis. Structure–activity insights highlight compound 10b as the most potent derivative, achieving strong growth inhibition in colorectal and breast cancer cell lines, while maintaining low cytotoxicity against normal cells. These findings emphasize the therapeutic potential of quinoxaline scaffolds for folate enzyme inhibition; however, current studies remain limited to in vitro assays and docking analyses, with no in vivo or clinical validation available. Future research should therefore expand SAR optimization, explore resistance mechanisms, and perform translational studies to determine the clinical efficacy and safety of these inhibitors.

sec.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitiors
sec.p: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) are protein kinases that control cell cycle and division (Peyressatre et al., 2015). It operates by binding cyclins to phosphorylate substrates to facilitate the transition through the different phases of the cell division cycle (Łukasik et al., 2021). In cancer, CDKs are abnormally activated and, therefore, promote cell growth in the body. Elevation in the levels of CDKs or increased activity of these proteins can lead to the breakdown of the cell checkpoints that are in place to control cell division and growth, and cancer cells are likely to proliferate more efficiently than normal cells (Łukasik et al., 2021). Quinoxaline compounds act as ATP-competitive inhibitors and have anticancer action via CDK inhibition. They bind to CDKs’ ATP-binding pockets, blocking ATP binding and limiting kinase activity. This inhibition can cause cell cycle arrest at various checkpoints, resulting in apoptosis in cancer cells (Fahmi et al., 2024).

A study by Lekgau (2021) reported that many quinoxaline compounds have shown potential as CDK inhibitors in cancer cells. An IC50 of 7.566 μM was shown by 2-(4,6-diamino-1,3,5-triazin-2-yl)phenol against CDK2. The pyrazolopyrimidine derivative dinaciclib, which hinders several CDKs such as CDK2, showed strong anti-proliferative effects with IC50 values in the low nanomolar range against different cancer cell lines. Another compound, 4-aminopyrido[2,3-d]pyrimidine, exhibited CDK2 inhibitory activity with an IC50 value of 0.01 μM. These CDK inhibitors based on quinoxaline usually function by competitively attaching to the ATP-binding pocket of CDK enzymes, blocking ATP binding and halting kinase activity and cell cycle progression. Different substituents can be fine-tuned for enhanced effectiveness and selectivity towards particular CDK isoforms, thanks to the planar quinoxaline core that enables advantageous interactions in the binding pocket.

The current evidence indicates that quinoxaline-based CDK inhibitors possess strong antiproliferative activity by competitively binding to ATP pockets and inducing cell cycle arrest. SAR findings suggest that derivatives with specific heteroaryl or diamino substitutions enhance inhibitory potency, achieving nanomolar IC₅₀ values in CDK2 assays. These results highlight the potential of quinoxaline scaffolds for selective CDK targeting; however, studies remain limited to in vitro evaluations, and further in vivo and mechanistic investigations are needed to establish their clinical relevance.

sec.title: Antiproliferative effects of quinoxaline derivatives on HIF-1α, VEGF, and p21
sec.p: HIF-1α is a key transcription factor that helps cells adapt to low oxygen conditions. It promotes tumor growth by inducing angiogenesis through VEGF. Moreover, VEGF is crucial for forming new blood vessels, which supports tumor development and metastasis. Additionally, P21, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, regulates the cell cycle and apoptosis, further influencing tumor growth. Targeting these factors, therefore, offers significant therapeutic potential in cancer treatment.

In a recent study by Ayoup et al. (2024b), a series of new quinoxaline derivatives were evaluated for their potential as anticancer agents by targeting HIF-1α, VEGF, and p21 in colorectal cancer. The research involved testing these compounds for cytotoxicity against normal colonic epithelial cells to assess their safety. Compounds with selectivity indices (Sis) of ≥3, including compounds 6, 9, 14, and 20 demonstrated notable selectivity towards cancer cells compared to normal cells, outperforming the reference drug doxorubicin. Among these, compound 21 showed the highest selectivity with an SI of 3.96 and exhibited the most significant anticancer activity with an IC50 of 0.029 μM against HCT-116 colorectal cancer cells. The study also revealed that compounds 6, 9, 14, and 20 effectively inhibited HIF-1α and VEGF expression while upregulating p21, thereby promoting apoptosis. These compounds induced significant morphological changes in cancer cells and displayed favorable drug-like properties and strong binding affinities to VEGFR-2, suggesting their potential as effective therapeutic agents in colorectal cancer treatment.

The current findings suggest that quinoxaline-based derivatives can effectively suppress tumor growth by simultaneously targeting HIF-1α, VEGF, and p21 pathways. Structure–activity insights highlight compound 21 as the most potent candidate, showing nanomolar IC₅₀ values and high selectivity for colorectal cancer cells. These results underscore the therapeutic promise of quinoxaline scaffolds in angiogenesis and cell-cycle regulation; however, the evidence is limited to a single study, and further in vivo and clinical investigations are necessary to validate their translational potential.

sec.title: MODIFICATION OF QUINOXALINE DERIVATIVES (SAR)
sec.p: A comprehensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis reveals that the biological activity of quinoxaline derivatives is strongly governed by the nature and position of substituents on the core scaffold. Across multiple studies, electronic effects, substitution patterns, and functional group orientation collectively modulate antiproliferative potency, selectivity, and overall anticancer efficacy.

From a position-specific perspective, substitutions at the C2 and C3 positions of the quinoxaline core primarily modulate target engagement and intrinsic potency. Bulky aryl or heteroaryl groups at these positions favor enhanced antiproliferative and kinase inhibitory activity by extending into enzyme binding pockets. In contrast, substitutions at the N1 and N4 positions predominantly influence pharmacokinetic-related properties, including solubility, cell permeability, and selectivity. The introduction of polar or bulky groups at N1/N4 has been shown to improve cellular uptake and, in some cases, enhance kinase selectivity.

Substitution on the phenyl ring attached to the quinoxaline core plays a decisive role in enhancing cytotoxic activity. In particular, electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) consistently improve antiproliferative effects across multiple cancer cell lines. This trend is exemplified by the study of (Pandiri et al., 2021), in which a series of quinoxaline derivatives (5a–5m) were evaluated against MCF-7, HeLa, A549, and IMR-32 cells. Among these, compound 5j, bearing 3,5-dichloro substituents on the phenyl ring, exhibited the highest antiproliferative activity and outperformed the reference drug etoposide across all tested cell lines. Compounds 5c (4-methoxy) and 5i (4-nitro) showed the next highest activities, whereas derivatives containing methyl, fluoro, cyano, or methoxy groups displayed only moderate to low cytotoxicity. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of electron-withdrawing substituents particularly meta-chloro groups in enhancing antiproliferative activity, likely through favorable electronic modulation and improved target engagement. The comparative in vitro anticancer activities of compounds 5c–5j are summarized in Table 7.

Position-specific modification of the quinoxaline nucleus further highlights the importance of substitution at heterocyclic sites. SAR analysis reported by Patinote et al. (2023) demonstrated that substitutions at the 1- and 4-positions of the [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinoxaline core are critical determinants of cytotoxic potency. Aromatic substituents at position 1 bearing hydrogen-bond donor or acceptor functionalities such as 3,4-dimethoxyphenyl (16a), 3-methoxyphenyl (16b), and 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl (17a), were associated with enhanced activity against A375 melanoma cells. In parallel, the presence of a methylamino group at position 4 was found to be essential for maintaining high potency. Notably, compound 17a, incorporating both a 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl group at position 1 and a methylamino substituent at position 4, emerged as the most potent analogue, exhibiting an EC₅₀ value of 365 nM. In contrast, derivatives lacking the methylamino group at position 4 or containing simple alkyl substituents showed markedly reduced or negligible activity. Additionally, heterocyclic substitutions at position 8 generally resulted in diminished potency, indicating limited tolerance for bulky or polar groups at this site.

Overall, the SAR trends observed across these studies highlight that optimal anticancer activity of quinoxaline derivatives arises from a synergistic combination of electronic modulation and position-specific substitution. Electron-withdrawing groups on peripheral aromatic rings enhance antiproliferative potency, while strategic substitution at the 1- and 4-positions of the quinoxaline scaffold, particularly the incorporation of hydrogen-bonding aromatic groups and methylamino functionalities is critical for achieving high activity. These insights provide a rational framework for the future design and optimization of quinoxaline-based anticancer agents with improved potency and selectivity. These SAR trends are summarized in a generalized SAR map in Fig. 5.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This systematic review comprehensively evaluates the anticancer potential of quinoxaline derivatives by analyzing studies published from 2020 to 2024. The findings highlight a multi-targeted profile, demonstrating that these compounds exert their effects through diverse mechanisms, including DNA intercalation, alkylation, antimetabolite activity, and inhibition of folate-pathway enzymes, which collectively interfere with DNA replication and repair, ultimately leading to cancer cell death. In particular, quinoxaline derivatives inhibit Topoisomerase II, stabilizing DNA enzyme complexes and preventing religation of DNA strands, which results in apoptosis. Furthermore, they target critical signaling proteins such as EGFR, HER2, VEGFR, BRD9, and CK2, contributing to the disruption of oncogenic signaling pathways, gene-expression regulation, and chromatin remodeling.

Structure-activity relationship (SAR) studies reveal that derivatives with aromatic substituents at specific positions, methylamino groups at position 4, and hydrogen bond donors or acceptors at position 1 exhibit higher anticancer activity, indicating opportunities for rational design and chemical optimization. Compared with previous reviews, which largely focused on individual mechanisms or select targets, this review integrates recent discoveries on emerging targets such as BRD9, BD1-selective BET, and PFKFB3, broadening the understanding of how quinoxaline derivatives can be strategically optimized for therapeutic applications. Recent preclinical studies demonstrate enhanced potency of newer derivatives, particularly against VEGFR-2, which has emerged as a critical target in resistant cancer cell lines. For example, compounds reported by Alsaif et al. (2022) inhibited VEGFR-2 with IC₅₀ values near 1 µM and significantly suppressed proliferation of HepG2, MCF-7, and HCT-116 cells. Similarly, (Alanazi et al., 2021a) reported compound 11e with an IC₅₀ of 2.1 nM against VEGFR-2, inducing G2/M cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis in both MCF-7 and HepG2 cells. These findings underscore the potential of quinoxaline derivatives to outperform certain approved TKIs such as sorafenib in select experimental settings

sec.title: Clinical perspective and translational outlook
sec.p: The preclinical findings presented in this review show that quinoxaline derivatives possess strong VEGFR-2 inhibitory activity and significant antiproliferative effects in multiple cancer cell lines, including those resistant to current TKIs. Although no quinoxaline-based anticancer agent has yet advanced to late phase clinical trials, these results suggest that optimized derivatives could complement or improve on approved tyrosine-kinase inhibitors such as lenvatinib or sorafenib, particularly for tumors that develop resistance to existing therapies. Progress toward clinical application will require well-designed animal studies to confirm antitumor efficacy and evaluate safety, followed by comprehensive pharmacokinetic and toxicological profiling to establish clinically relevant dosing. Parallel investigations of combination strategies such as pairing quinoxaline VEGFR-2 inhibitors with immune-checkpoint inhibitors or EGFR blockers could determine whether these agents provide synergistic benefit and help overcome acquired resistance.

sec.title: Challenges and future directions
sec.p: While quinoxaline derivatives demonstrate broad anticancer activity in vitro, translating these findings into clinical benefit requires overcoming several scientific and practical hurdles. Pharmacokinetics and bioavailability remain poorly defined, with only a few reports providing preliminary ADME or metabolic stability data and no comprehensive animal pharmacokinetic studies available. Without these data, it is difficult to determine clinically relevant dosing or predict potential off-target toxicity.

Physicochemical properties are likely to contribute substantially to these translational limitations. Many potent quinoxaline analogues are characterized by highly aromatic and lipophilic scaffolds, features that are commonly associated with elevated LogP/LogD values and limited polar surface area (TPSA), when such parameters are reported. These properties are well known to impair aqueous solubility, oral absorption, and formulation feasibility, while increasing plasma protein binding. In addition, the presence of heteroaromatic cores with basic functionalities raises concerns regarding hERG-related cardiotoxicity, a frequent cause of late-stage attrition among kinase- and DNA-targeting small molecules. Metabolic instability, including rapid oxidative metabolism and CYP-mediated clearance, may further limit in vivo exposure despite strong in vitro potency.

Drug delivery challenges further complicate development, as poor aqueous solubility restricts systemic administration. Advanced delivery strategies, such as lipid nanoparticles, polymeric micelles, or prodrug approaches, which have shown success for other heteroaromatic anticancer agents, could potentially enhance solubility, tumor accumulation, and therapeutic index of quinoxaline derivatives, yet remain underexplored for this scaffold.

Beyond conventional small-molecule optimization, emerging therapeutic modalities offer new opportunities to enhance the translational potential of quinoxaline derivatives. One such strategy involves proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), which are bifunctional molecules designed to induce selective degradation of disease-related proteins rather than merely inhibiting their activity (Sakamoto et al., 2001). In this context, quinoxaline-based kinase inhibitors could serve as effective warheads within PROTAC systems, provided that solvent-exposed positions on the scaffold allow linker attachment without compromising target binding.

In addition, highly potent quinoxaline derivatives that interfere with tubulin polymerization or DNA-associated processes may be explored as payloads in antibody–drug conjugates (ADCs). ADCs combine a cytotoxic small molecule with a tumor-targeting monoclonal antibody, enabling selective delivery to cancer cells and potentially reducing systemic toxicity. Incorporating quinoxaline-based cytotoxins into such targeted platforms could significantly expand their therapeutic window and clinical applicability.

Mechanistic gaps also persist. Most apoptosis studies focus narrowly on caspase activation without distinguishing between intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and only a few extend beyond VEGFR-2 or Topoisomerase II. Expanding mechanistic investigations to include immune-modulatory effects, metabolic reprogramming, and tumor–microenvironment interactions may reveal additional therapeutic opportunities.

Finally, combination strategies warrant focused evaluation. Early cell-based studies suggest potential synergy between quinoxaline-based VEGFR inhibitors and EGFR blockade, and there is strong rationale for pairing these compounds with immune checkpoint inhibitors to overcome resistance to standard TKIs. Addressing these gaps through comprehensive in vivo studies, detailed pharmacokinetic profiling, optimized drug-delivery systems, and rational combination regimens will be critical to advance quinoxaline derivatives from promising laboratory agents to clinically viable anticancer therapeutics.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This systematic review underscores the promising anticancer potential of quinoxaline derivatives, a diverse class of heterocyclic compounds exhibiting efficacy across various cancer types. While previous reviews have largely concentrated on mechanisms such as topoisomerase inhibition and DNA intercalation, our analysis of 77 studies published between 2020 and 2024 broadens this perspective by identifying additional molecular targets, including BRD9, BD1-selective BET, and PFKFB3, which were not addressed in earlier reviews. We also provide deeper insights into the role of quinoxaline derivatives as antimetabolites, particularly in inhibiting enzymes associated with the folate pathway-an area less explored in prior research. Beyond their established activities of inhibiting VEGFR, EGFR, and HER2, our review highlights the emerging role of these compounds in targeting novel signaling pathways and proteins, thereby enhancing their therapeutic potential. In conclusion, quinoxaline derivatives represent a promising direction for anticancer therapy due to their diverse biological activities and effectiveness as molecular inhibitors. However, further research is crucial to fully elucidate their mechanisms and address existing limitations, which could pave the way for developing more effective and safer cancer therapies in the future.
